questionStem: Six days after undergoing an operation for a truncus arteriosus defect , an 8-day-old newborn appears jittery. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F) , pulse is 130/min, respirations are 44/min , and blood pressure is 70/58 mm Hg. Examination shows micrognathia and hypertelorism . His serum calcium concentration is 7 mg/dl. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly without a thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is a disorder caused by a microdeletion in the 22q11.2 chromosome, which results in abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. It presents early in childhood with thymic hypoplasia and impaired immunity, conotruncal cardiac defects (eg, truncus arteriosus), hypocalcemia caused by parathyroid hypoplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities, such as low set ears, hypertelorism, micrognathia, and cleft lip and palate. It is associated with developmental delay. Laboratory evaluation will show leukopenia and decreased calcium concentrations, while a chest x-ray may demonstrate the absence of a thymic shadow, as in this patient. Further evaluation typically includes an echocardiography and kidney ultrasonography. Treatment is supportive. This patient presenting with jitteriness in the setting of hypocalcemia and truncus arteriosus likely has DiGeorge syndrome, making hypoparathyroidism the most likely diagnosis. Severe hypocalcemia can also present with seizures, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, and emesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Hyperparathyroidism {Choice A), when primary, presents with hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma, and less likely hyperplasia or carcinoma. Hypercalcemia presents with abdominal pain, nephrolithiasis, bone pain, and altered mental status. Secondary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, but this usually occurs in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Pseudohypoparathyroidism {Choice C) is caused by an impaired response of the kidney to parathyroid hormone, which results in hypocalcemia. It is commonly associated with short stature, developmental delay, and osteodystrophy as part of a genetic disorder referred to as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. It is not associated with cardiac defects. Renal proximal tubular dysfunction {Choice D) commonly causes a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis as a result of an inability to reabsorb sodium bicarbonate. It can be a symptom of Fanconi syndrome, which also presents with hypophosphatemic rickets and growth delay. Vitamin D-deficient rickets {Choice E) presents with hypocalcemia and bone weakening that can lead to deformities such as genu varum. It is usually secondary to a prolonged deficiency of Vitamin D and would not be expected to present at birth. X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets {Choice F) is caused by an inherited inability of the renal proximal tubule to reabsorb phosphate and presents similarly to vitamin D-deficient rickets. It would not be expected to cause such a severe decrease in blood calcium concentrations. Educational Objective: DiGeorge syndrome presents with thymic hypoplasia and impaired immunity, conotruncal cardiac defects, hypocalcemia caused by parathyroid hypoplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities. Parathyroid hypoplasia can lead to severe hypocalcemia after birth, with symptoms of neuromuscular instability and, occasionally, seizures.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea containing blood and mucus . He has a history of recurrent ear infections treated with antibiotics . He completed a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 day ago. He appears moderately ill. His temperature is 38.4°C (101 .1 °F), pulse is 104lmin , respirations are 20lmin , and blood pressure is 100162 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows moderate left lower quadrant tenderness with no rebound . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Test of the stool for occult blood is positive . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Clostridium difficile infection is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics, classically ampicillin and clindamycin, as a result of the loss of native colonic microbiota. This derangement in native microbiota presents an opportunity for the competition-free proliferation of C. difficile, which produces toxins that result in dysfunction of the brush border and a subsequent secretory diarrhea. C. difficile infections are associated with the presence of pseudomembranes that appear as patchy regions of white mucosa on colonoscopy. The severity of C. difficile colitis can vary, ranging from watery diarrhea and abdominal pain without constitutional symptoms in mild cases to toxic megacolon, colonic ischemia, and severe sepsis in fulminant cases. Treatment includes oral or rectal vancomycin, intravenous or oral metronidazole, fidaxomicin, or colectomy depending on the severity of the patient's presentation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Salmonella enteritidis (Choice B) is a gram-negative rod that can cause enteritis, presenting with watery diarrhea, cramping, and abdominal pain. It does not occur secondary to the use of antibiotics. Exposure to Salmonella enteritidis commonly occurs through inadequately cooked eggs or chicken. Shigella sonnei (Choice C) is a gram-negative rod that can cause bloody diarrhea with systemic symptoms such as fever and myalgias. Bloody stools caused by shigellosis are often more frankly bloody than those of C. difficile colitis and often contain mucus or pus. Shigellosis does not occur secondary to the use of antibiotics. Staphylococcus aureus (Choice D) can cause enteritis, which presents with vomiting, diarrhea, and dehydration. Symptoms are typically self-limited and resolve over 1 to 2 days. It results as a consequence of eating contaminated food (food poisoning) and is generally caused by exotoxin production. Yersinia enterocolitica (Choice E) is a gram-negative rod that causes bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. It results as a consequence of eating contaminated food or water. Educational Objective: Clostridium difficile infection is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics as a result of the loss of native colonic microbiota that allows competition-free proliferation of C. difficile. Patients typically present with watery diarrhea and abdominal pain; however, the diarrhea can become bloody and result in fulminant symptoms such as toxic megacolon and sepsis if severe.

questionStem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection . Over the past 15 months, she has had several episodes of acute otitis media. She is afebrile . On examination , she is alert and turns her head appropriately in response to sounds . The left external ear and canal appear normal. The left tympanic membrane is bluish gray with visible landmarks ; an air-fluid level is present behind the inferior half of the tympanic membrane . There is minimal movement on pneumatic otoscopy . The right external ear, ear canal, and tympanic membrane appear normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.H: Retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane

correctExplanation: Serous otitis media is suggested by the presence of a middle ear effusion in the absence of signs of acute otitis media. Eustachian tube obstruction or dysfunction leads to the accumulation of serous fluid within the middle ear. Such dysfunction is common in the setting of an upper respiratory tract infection because of the inflammation of the nasal mucosa occluding the ostium of the eustachian tube. Fluid accumulation typically presents with hearing loss, ear tugging, or vertigo. Patients with serous otitis media lack findings of fever, tympanic membrane erythema, or retrotympanic pus, which are more commonly found in the presence of acute otitis media. Treatment is supportive, as the condition is usually self-limited.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Acoustic neuroma (Choice A) may present with chronic sensorineural deafness or vertigo. They are often small, located near the cerebellopontine angle, and are associated with neurofibromatosis. Fluid in the middle ear cavity would not be expected. Acute otitis media (Choice B) classically occurs in children, often from viral or bacterial pathogens. It presents with ear pain, fever, and an erythematous tympanic membrane with retrotympanic pus or middle ear effusion. Bell palsy (Choice C), also known as facial (nerve) palsy, may result from viral infection or inflammation of the nerve and presents with unilateral weakness of the facial muscles including those of the forehead. Benign positional vertigo (Choice D) results from translocation of an otolith into the semicircular canals and presents with acute episodes of postural vertigo. Cholesteatoma (Choice E) is the accumulation of keratin and keratinized squamous epithelium within the middle ear and presents with mild, moderate, or severe conductive hearing loss, and occasionally with ipsilateral pain if the lesion has invaded surrounding structures. Mastoiditis (Choice F) describes bacterial infection of the mastoid air cells. It results from untreated or recurrent otitis media and presents with postauricular pain, swelling, and erythema. Perforation of the tympanic membrane (Choice G) results in acute conductive hearing loss and would be visible on otoscopic examination. Retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane (Choice H) results from chronic otitis media and may result in hearing loss if the architecture of the ossicles is disrupted. Acute serous effusion does not result directly from tympanic membrane retraction.

questionStem: A healthy 16-year-old girl comes to the physician for an examination prior to participation in school sports. She had chickenpox at the age of 3 years but has no other history of serious illness . Her immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten ; the only immunization she has received since then is a diphtheria-tetanus toxoid at the age of 10 years for a laceration on her leg. She has been sexually active for the past year with two male partners who have used condoms consistently . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m 2• Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities . Administration of which of the following vaccines is most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: Hepatitis B, diphtheria-tetanus-toxoid (Td), and human papillomavirus (HPV)
choices.D: Pneumococcal conjugate , 7-valent (PCV-7); inactivated poliovirus (IPV); and hepatitis B

correctExplanation: The most appropriate vaccine series for this patient would include human papillomavirus (HPV), meningococcal, and tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (TdaP) vaccines. HPV is a nonenveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the papillomaviridae family that causes genital warts. Infection with HPV is a significant and preventable risk factor for cervical, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal cancer. Administration of the HPV vaccine is recommended for both male and female patients between the ages of 9 and 26 years. For both sexes, it provides protection against genital warts, with the additional benefit of decreased cervical cancer risk in women. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine is indicated for all children, with an additional serogroup B vaccine indicated for all children over 10 years old at increased risk for meningococcal disease (eg, dormitory, military living). This would be appropriate in this patient who may attend college and participate in dormitory living. Although the patient received the diphtheria-tetanus toxoid (Td) at the age of 10 years, she will need the TdaP vaccine. Children receive a childhood series of immunization for diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus (DTaP) involving pertussis antigens. The TdaP includes a tetanus toxoid, decreased diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis and is recommended for adolescents starting at age 11 years.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Hepatitis B immunization (Choices A, C, and D) is typically administered to newborns or to adults who previously did not receive the vaccine. The patient's immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten, meaning she likely received the hepatitis B vaccine as a newborn. The Td booster (Choices A and F) is recommended every 10 years for adults who have previously received the TdaP vaccine. Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) (Choices C and F) is a routine vaccination that involves two doses: one at 12 to 15 months and one between 4 to 6 years. The patient's immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten, meaning she likely received the MMR vaccine. Pneumococcal conjugate, 7-valent (PCV-7), and inactivated poliovirus (IPV) (Choices D and E) would also not be indicated in this patient. PCV-7 was the first pneumococcal vaccine that provided protection against seven serotypes of pneumococcal bacteria. The current pneumococcal vaccine is PCV-13, which provides further protection with six other serotypes. It is typically given at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months of age. IPV is similarly given at 2, 4, 6 to 18 months old, and 4 through 6 years old. Given that the patient has received all vaccines prior to kindergarten, she likely already has had these immunizations. Educational Objective: Adolescents should receive immunizations against HPV and meningococcus, and a booster for tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of progressive tiredness during the past month . She received the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus 4 years ago and takes insulin twice daily; she has never missed a dose. Two weeks ago, her hemoglobin A,c was 6%. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications . She has had no changes in appetite or weight. Menarche occurred at the age of 13 years . Menses occur at irregular 30- to 40-day intervals . For the past 3 months, they have lasted longer, and the flow has been heavier. Her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. Her pulse is 60/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is easily palpated . The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 4. Serum studies are most likely to show an increased concentration of which of the following hormones?
correctExplanation: Hypothyroidism classically presents with a combination of fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and may demonstrate heavy or irregular periods. Physical examination may show bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. In this patient, her symptoms of tiredness, progressively heavier and irregular periods (menometrorrhagia), and bradycardia, in the setting of a preexisting autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes mellitus) suggests the presence of a second autoimmune condition, likely acquired hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto thyroiditis. While many causes of hypothyroidism exist, Hashimoto disease is a common cause of painless thyroiditis, which may present with a palpable, enlarged thyroid gland, as in this patient. With progressive inflammation and destruction of the thyroid parenchyma, circulating concentrations of thyroxine and triiodothyronine decrease, with resulting feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary leading to increased concentrations of thyrotropin­ releasing hormone (TRH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and prolactin. The increased TSH concentration is measurable in serum and provides ongoing trophic stimulation to the thyroid gland. Increased prolactin may cause breast development, galactorrhea, and may promote irregular anovulatory cycles or amenorrhea through feedback on gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Treatment includes supplementation with levothyroxine and frequent follow-up visits to evaluate for therapeutic effectiveness, including monitoring of serum TSH concentration.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cortisol (Choice A) is increased in primary and secondary Cushing syndrome, often caused by a hyperfunctioning adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, or an adrenocorticotropin-secreting tumor. Its concentrations are generally not affected, or may be only mildly deviated from normal limits, in the setting of hypothyroidism. Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (Choice B) is an androgen produced by the adrenal zona reticularis. It may be increased in cases of polycystic ovarian syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and Cushing disease, though is more often used to identify a source of hyperandrogenism in patients with virilization, precocious puberty, or infertility. When increased, the adrenal gland is likely the source of the endogenous increase in steroid synthesis, and when normal, the source is often a functional ovarian or testicular tumor. Estrogen (Choice C) is a steroid produced by the theca cells of the ovary. It promotes bone development and regulates endometrial development during the menstrual cycle. This patient's irregular cycles are more attributable to the effects of hypothyroidism and prolactin than to deranged estrogen synthesis. Luteinizing (Choice D) hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and, along with follicle-stimulating hormone, controls the ovarian cycle. It increases sharply around the midpoint of the menstrual cycle, triggering ovulation. Its concentrations may be decreased in hypothyroidism as a result of the negative feedback from potentially increased prolactin. Educational Objective: Hypothyroidism classically presents with a combination of fatigue, weight gain, constipation, and cold intolerance, and it may demonstrate heavy or irregular periods. Physical examination may show bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a common cause of primary hypothyroidism, especially in patients with a history of autoimmune disease. Serum TSH concentration is generally increased, while concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased.

questionStem: A 2-month -old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a well-child examination . He was born at 39 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight and 75th percentile for head circumference . His rectal temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 45/min . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97% at the right thumb and 98% at the left thumb and right great toe. The apical impulse is prominent , and there is a thrill in the second left intercostal space . There is a continuous "machinery-like" murmur increasing in intensity during systole and waning during diastole ; it is loudest in the second left intercostal space and radiates down the left sternal border. Peripheral pulses are 4+ in all extremities . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: A patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) presents with a heart murmur described as a continuous "machinery-like" murmur best heard in the left second intercostal and left infraclavicular regions. Since blood flow through the PDA occurs in both systole and diastole, the sound will be present throughout the cardiac cycle. The ductus arteriosus is one of several physiologic shunts existing during the prenatal period. In utero, oxygenated blood is obtained from the placenta, not from the lungs, and the ductus arteriosus (DA) allows the shunting of oxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery directly to the aorta while bypassing the fetal lungs, which are filled with amniotic fluid. At birth, closure of the DA occurs by the release of prostaglandins and increased arterial oxygen tension. With increased blood oxygenation and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance following birth or with indomethacin use, prostaglandin production falls and the ductus closes. Certain congenital heart diseases require the presence of a shunt to allow arteriovenous admixture of oxygenated blood, for example, transposition of the great vessels. In the absence of such a requirement for shunting, a PDA results in a chronic extracardiac left-to-right shunt that may result in pulmonary hypertension or right-sided heart failure, with the risk for Eisenmenger syndrome if uncorrected. PDAs that are small often go undetected until adulthood because the left-to-right shunt is not significant enough to cause symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Extracardiac right-to-left shunt {Choice B) occurs in the setting of a chronic left-to-right shunt that results in increased pulmonary blood flow and progression of pulmonary hypertension with consequent Eisenmenger syndrome and reversal of the shunt. This may occur in the setting of a chronic, uncorrected PDA. An extracardiac right-to-left shunt can also occur in pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are a characteristic finding in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, which typically presents with recurrent hemoptysis and an increased risk for paradoxical emboli. lntracardiac atrial left-to-right shunt {Choice C) occurs with an atrial septal defect (ASD), which is a common congenital malformation of the interatrial septum. It classically presents with a fixed, split S2 as a result of increased blood flow across the pulmonic valve, and a low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation. lntracardiac atrial right-to-left shunt {Choice D) may result from a chronic, uncorrected ASD that progresses to Eisenmenger syndrome. lntracardiac ventricular left-to-right shunt {Choice E) occurs with a ventricular septal defect (VSD), which is characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border. lntracardiac ventricular right-to-left shunt {Choice F) may occur with a chronic, uncorrected VSD that progresses to Eisenmenger syndrome. Educational Objective: A PDA results from failure of the normal, extracardiac embryonic shunt between the pulmonary artery and aorta to appropriately close in the neonatal period. It results in an extracardiac left-to­ right shunt and classically presents with a continuous machine-like murmur.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of headaches that have increased in frequency and severity over the past month. She began working at a health food store 2 months ago and has been taking several vitamin supplements including A, B6, C, D, and E. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 78/min , respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows mild papilledema . Neurologic examination shows no focal findings . A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities . A lumbar puncture is performed ; cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows no abnormalities other than increased opening pressure . An excess intake of which of the following vitamins is the most likely explanation for this patient's condition ?
correctExplanation: Pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension {IIH), is characterized by signs of increased intracranial pressure including headache, papilledema, and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture without any underlying pathology to cause such findings on neuroimaging. It is primarily seen in young women who are overweight. Although there is no malignant cause underlying the increased intracranial pressure, it may cause debilitating headaches and permanent vision loss. Headaches that are secondary to increased intracranial pressure often are worse when lying down and relieved by standing. The most common risk factors for the development of pseudotumor cerebri include female sex and obesity. However, hypervitaminosis A from increased dietary intake is another potential cause of IIH. This can be from excessive dietary intake or from the use of retinoid medications such as isotretinoin or all-trans retinoic acid. Other medications associated with IIH include tetracyclines, danazol, and oral contraceptives.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is not associated with increased B-complex vitamins including B6 (pyridoxine) {Choice B). Because B-complex vitamins and vitamin C {Choice C) are water soluble and thus easily excreted in the urine, conditions caused by an excess of these vitamins are rare. Neither are associated with IIH. Vitamin D {Choice D) and vitamin E {Choice E) are, like vitamin A, fat-soluble. Excessive amounts of these vitamins can develop from exogenous supplementation, which may sometimes be seen in fad dieters. Excessive vitamin D induces hypercalcemia and its manifestations such as confusion, polyuria, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness, and nephrolithiasis. Excessive vitamin E may alter the metabolism of vitamin K, enhancing the anticoagulant effects of warfarin in a patient taking this medication. Neither predispose to the development of IIH. Educational Objective: Pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension {IIH), presents with headache, papilledema, and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture in young, obese women without any underlying mass on neuroimaging. Hypervitaminosis A is associated with an increased risk for the development of IIH.

questionStem: A 2-week-old newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-day history of excessive forceful vomiting after eating . The vomitus is not green or bloody. He continues to breast feed vigorously but has had fewer wet diapers than normal. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. He appears mildly dehydrated . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and pulse is 135/min. The abdomen is soft, and the patient tolerates deep palpation of the abdomen without crying . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non bloody, non bilious emesis after feedings, and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated bouts of vomiting can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by the loss of hydrochloric acid and volume contraction. On physical examination, an ovoid lump may be palpated in the upper abdomen, which correlates with the hypertrophied pylorus. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is by abdominal ultrasonography demonstrating thickened pyloric musculature. Treatment is with a surgical pyloromyotomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. X-ray of the abdomen (Choice A) may show distention of the stomach in pyloric stenosis and can also be used to evaluate other intra-abdominal pathology, such as bowel obstruction. However, it would not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. X-ray of the chest (Choice B) is used in the evaluation of chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough to assess for intrathoracic pathology. Upright chest x-ray is also used in suspected cases of bowel perforation. It is not commonly used to evaluate recurrent emesis in absence of suspected complications, although it could demonstrate a hiatal or diaphragmatic hernia if present. It plays no role in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Barium enema (Choice C) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine, such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. CT scan of the abdomen (Choice E) would likely demonstrate the hypertrophic pyloric musculature. However, it is associated with a much greater radiation exposure than ultrasonography, making it a less appropriate next step in diagnosis. Educational Objective: Pyloric stenosis presents at several weeks of life and is characterized by repeated nonbilious vomiting after feeds, leading to dehydration and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, and treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing for 2 hours. He also has had low-grade fever, nasal congestion , and a runny nose for 2 days. He is in mild respiratory distress . His temperature is 38.3°C (101 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 48/min . Generalized harsh breath sounds and inspiratory stridor are heard on auscultation ; inspiratory stridor can be heard without the use of a stethoscope . Which of the following is the most likely site of pathology in this patient?
correctExplanation: Stridor refers to a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow through obstructed or narrowed upper airway structures, such as the pharynx, larynx, or trachea. It can be caused by illnesses such as croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or epiglottitis, or by structural lesions such as a laryngeal tumor, foreign body, tracheomalacia, or laryngospasm. This patient presenting with a new fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and respiratory distress is likely suffering an acute infection involving the structures of the larynx. Croup is characterized by fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. Illness is typically mild and self-limited; however, inflammation of the upper airway can result in life-threatening airway obstruction. It can be caused by viral or bacterial infections, commonly parainfluenza virus. Plain x-rays may disclose subglottic narrowing of the airway.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Alveoli and interstitial tissues (Choice A) are inflamed in pneumonia. Pneumonia characteristically presents with cough, fever, and areas of opacification on chest x-rays. Pulmonary auscultation may disclose crackles, wheezes, or decreased breath sounds. Stridor is associated with inflammation of the upper airway. Bronchi (Choice B) are inflamed in bronchitis, which is a common cause of cough in young children. Typical respiratory pathogens causing bronchitis are viruses, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxel/a catarrhalis. Stridor may affect portions of the bronchi, although it is centered in the upper airways of the larynx and trachea. Bronchioles (Choice C) are inflamed in bronchiolitis, which is a common lower respiratory tract infection in children younger than 2 years of age, classically caused by respiratory syncytial virus. Auscultation may disclose wheezes and crackles. Chest wall (Choice D) pathology may result in stridor in the setting of external compression of the airway from a chest wall mass or an enlarging abscess. Croup is a more likely diagnosis in this patient with acute symptoms. Educational Objective: Laryngotracheobronchitis, also known as croup, typically presents with fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. It is commonly secondary to a viral infection from parainfluenza. Stridor refers to a high-pitched sound secondary to turbulent airflow from an underlying upper airway obstruction, often caused by inflammation (epiglottitis, laryngitis, tracheitis) or structural lesions (foreign body, laryngeal tumor).

questionStem: A healthy 1-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of pallor for 2 weeks . Her immunizations are up-to-date . She was fed commercial formula until the age of 6 months and has been fed 2% cow's milk and table food since then . Development has been normal. She is at the 50th percentile for height and the 90th percentile for weight. Hematocrit is 26%. A blood smear with Wright stain is shown . Supplementation with which of the following is most likely to have prevented this condition?
correctExplanation: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) presents with microcytic, hypochromic anemia with otherwise normal shape of red blood cells. IDA is extremely prevalent worldwide, especially in developing countries, in pregnant women, and in children. Infants and children are particularly vulnerable to IDA as a result of rapid growth and dietary deficiencies. The patient has been fed primarily cow's milk for the past 6 months, along with table food, while formula was stopped at 6 months of age. This places the infant at risk for iron deficiency given the insufficient amount of iron in cow's milk. Many types of formulas and foods are fortified with iron to ensure appropriate supplementation. Iron is required for the synthesis of heme, which is a necessary component of the hemoglobin molecule, and thus, of erythrocytes. It functions to shuttle oxygen to and from peripheral tissues. Erythrocytes on the peripheral blood smear are hypochromic as a result of deficient hemoglobin concentration. It is hypothesized that erythrocytes are microcytic as a result of continuing erythrocyte division in order to reach an adequate hemoglobin concentration. Because hemoglobin stores are inadequate, cell division continues beyond what would normally occur and causes the cells to be smaller than normal. Treatment in the case of poor dietary intake is with oral iron supplementation. If severe, parenteral iron can be administered.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Folic acid (Choice A) deficiency presents with macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia. Folic acid deficiency may be observed in infants with malabsorptive diseases, such as celiac disease, or who are fed goat's milk, which contains insufficient concentrations of folic acid. Phosphatidylcholine (Choice C) is an important component of pulmonary surfactant. Deficiency presents with respiratory distress syndrome and is common in premature neonates. Phosphatidylcholine deficiency is not typically accompanied by anemia. Vitamin B6 (Choice D), or pyridoxine, deficiency is uncommon in children and infants and may present with seizures, peripheral neuropathy, and sideroblastic anemia. Vitamin E (Choice E) is an antioxidant that protects cells from free radical damage. Deficiency may present with hemolytic anemia and generalized muscle weakness. Vitamin E deficiency may occur in the neonatal period, especially in premature infants, but is less common in infancy. Educational Objective: Iron deficiency anemia presents with hypochromic, microcytic erythrocytes on peripheral smear. Iron deficiency is prevalent in children as a result of insufficient dietary intake, especially in children primarily fed cow's milk without iron-fortified formula or food supplementation. It is treated with oral iron supplementation.

questionStem: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 1-day history of fever, vomiting , and fussiness . He was born at 39 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He is alert and mildly irritable but easily consoled by his mother. His rectal temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 160/min, and respirations are 38/min. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities . The tympanic membranes are mildly erythematous with normal landmarks and motility. The lungs are clear to auscultation . The abdomen is soft with no palpable masses . The patient is uncircumcised . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11 .9 g/dL Leukocyte count 12,200/mm 3 Platelet count 240,000/mm 3 Urine Nitrites 2+ Leukocyte esterase 3+ Results of blood and urine cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Urinary tract infections are characterized by dysuria, urinary urgency, frequency, or incontinence. In infants, urinary tract infections may present solely with fever, irritability, or fussiness. Urinalysis often shows leukocytes, bacteria, and the presence of nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Risk factors for urinary tract infections include being less than 1 year of age, female, or an uncircumcised male. It should also be suspected especially when there is no other source of infection identified, such as otitis media or upper respiratory tract infection. Urinary tract infections should be treated with antibiotics with sufficient coverage of gram­ negative rods. Cefotaxime is a third-generation cephalosporin that would be sufficient to treat this patient's urinary tract infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cefazolin (Choice A) is a first-generation cephalosporin. It does have some activity against E. coli but lacks activity against many gram-negative rods. First-generation cephalosporins may be appropriate for a urinary tract infection if culture and sensitivity data support a susceptible organism. A third-generation cephalosporin is a broader choice. Nafcillin (Choice C) is used to treat gram-positive organisms, especially methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. It would not be the antibiotic of choice in a urinary tract infection, which is typically caused by gram­ negative rods. Similarly, penicillin (Choice D) may be inadequate to treat this urinary tract infection as it has limited coverage of gram-negative bacteria. Vancomycin (Choice E) inhibits bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan formation in gram-positive bacteria by binding to D-Ala-D-Ala. It is effective in the treatment of resistant organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and ampicillin-resistant Enterococcus species. It does not have significant activity against gram-negative pathogens. Educational Objective: In infants, urinary tract infections may present solely with fever, irritability, or fussiness. Urinalysis often shows leukocytes, bacteria, and the presence of nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Urinary tract infections should be treated with antibiotics with sufficient coverage of gram-negative rods.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after the onset of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 5 minutes . He has hypertension treated with a calcium-channel blocking agent , but he has not been taking his medication . On arrival , he is unarousable . His blood pressure is 250/154 mm Hg. Examination shows proliferative retinopathy . Urinalysis shows 1 + protein. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy may result from acute and severe increases in blood pressure. It may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure and may progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical hypertension or from hypertensive retinopathy. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with further gradual correction over the following day or more. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator and is a preferred agent because of its very short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Diazoxide (Choice A) is also a potent vasodilator and is occasionally used for the treatment of hypertensive emergency. However, its longer half-life makes it less optimal in comparison to nitroprusside. Furosemide (Choice B) is a loop diuretic. It is not typically used as a primary agent in the treatment of hypertensive emergency. Hydralazine (Choice C) is an effective agent for lowering blood pressure. However, it has a long half-life and its efficacy is often unpredictable, which may lead to unintended precipitous drops in blood pressure. Lorazepam (Choice D) is useful for the treatment of seizures, including status epilepticus. This patient's obtundation occurs, however, in the setting of extreme hypertension with potential cerebral edema, which is a more likely cause of his seizure than primary epilepsy. With correction of the blood pressure, further seizure activity should resolve. Educational Objective: Hypertensive encephalopathy requires the careful lowering of blood pressure, which must be done quickly while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator and is a preferred agent in this scenario because of its short half-life, allowing for the careful titration via intravenous infusion.

questionStem: A 1-month-old infant has had a 12 x 8-cm , red, raised, well-defined lesion that is lobulated and compressible overlying the buttocks since birth. Examination also shows multiple petechiae and bruises . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.C: Impaired tissue growth due to altered vascular supply
choices.D: Increased tissue growth due to increased vascular supply

correctExplanation: Vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma are rare in infancy. Tufted hemangiomas present as firm, red lesions with ill-defined borders on the arms, legs, and trunk, often sparing the head and face. They become larger, darker, and indurated with age, although most stabilize in childhood. Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma is a subcutaneous vascular mass that appears as a purpuric raised lesion, most commonly on the extremities. It also tends to become darker and indurated with time. Both of these vascular tumors are associated with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, which presents with bleeding, ecchymoses, and petechiae as a result of platelet sequestration by the tumor and an associated coagulopathy. Development of this syndrome typically presents with a rapid enlargement of the tumor, thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, and increased □-dimer concentration. Treatment options include steroids, chemotherapy (eg, vincristine), and immunomodulators (eg, sirolimus).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice A) presents with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, increased prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, decreased plasma fibrinogen concentration, and increased □- dimer concentration. It can be caused by trauma, severe sepsis, and, occasionally, malignancy. It is less likely than Kasabach-Merritt syndrome in this otherwise healthy patient with a vascular tumor. High-output congestive heart failure (Choice B) presents with shortness of breath, weight gain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and peripheral edema, often in the setting of an arteriovenous fistula, cirrhosis, sepsis, or severe anemia. It does not present with bruising and petechiae. Impaired tissue growth due to altered vascular supply (Choice C) and increased tissue growth due to increased vascular supply (Choice D) are incorrect, as the altered vascular supply to the vascular tumor does not affect tissue growth. Rather, the altered vasculature sequesters and activates platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy. Educational Objective: Vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas can be complicated by Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, which refers to the sequestration and activation of platelets by the tumor, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of leg pain during the past 3 months . The pain is predominantly in her calves ; it only occurs at night and often awakens her from sleep . The pain is exacerbated when she has been particularly active during the day and resolves with acetaminophen use and massage . She appears well. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F) , pulse is 108/min , respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities .

choices.E: lliotibial band syndrome M) Rheumatoid arthritis
choices.G: Osgood-Schlatter disease 0) Subluxation of the patella

correctExplanation: Growing pains are a common cause of musculoskeletal pain in children. The pain has characteristic features, including a bilateral, nonarticular presentation, commonly in the thighs or calves, and commonly occurs in the evening or at night. The cause of growing pains is unknown, as the pain does not typically occur at the sites of bone growth. Physical examination is normal and does not show any evidence of bone or joint inflammation or malformation. Patients do not usually have impairment of physical activity. The pain usually resolves by morning and treatment is symptomatic with massage, acetaminophen, and reassurance.
incorrectExplanation: , M, N, 0, P. Chondromalacia of the patella (Choice A) is a cartilaginous injury that may cause anterior knee pain. It most commonly occurs as an overuse injury in athletes. Discitis (Choice B) is an infection of the intervertebral disc. It may present in children with back pain and refusal to walk. Hypermobility syndrome (Choice D) presents with joint hypermobility and associated joint and muscle pain. lliotibial band syndrome (Choice E) is caused by friction between the iliotibial band and lateral femoral epicondyle. It occurs most commonly as an overuse injury in athletes and presents with lateral knee pain. Ligamentous injury (Choice F) of the knee, such as injury to the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments, typically occurs as an acute sports injury and presents with abrupt knee pain and swelling. Osgood-Schlatter disease (Choice G) refers to osteochondrosis or traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that typically occurs in adolescent, athletic children. It presents with anterior knee pain and swelling. Osteoid osteoma (Choice H) are benign bony tumors that commonly occur in long bones and present with pain and refusal to bear weight. The pain would not likely be bilateral. Osteomyelitis (Choice I) is an infection of bone and bone marrow, and typically presents acutely, subacutely, or chronically from direct inoculation or hematogenous spread. Patients typically complain of pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema.

questionStem: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician 24 hours after the onset of fever and increasingly severe left knee pain and swelling . She was unable to sleep last night because of the pain . She appears uncomfortable and is unable to bear weight on her left leg. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101 .7°F) , pulse is 112/min , respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 96/56 mm Hg. On examination , the left knee is swollen , red, warm , and exquisitely tender . She holds the knee in 45 degrees of flexion . She refuses to move the knee and resists passive extension and flexion . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities .

choices.E: lliotibial band syndrome M) Rheumatoid arthritis
choices.G: Osgood-Schlatter disease 0) Subluxation of the patella

incorrectExplanation: , M, 0, P. Chondromalacia of the patella (Choice A) is a cartilaginous injury that may cause anterior knee pain. It most commonly occurs as an overuse injury in athletes. Discitis (Choice B) is an infection of the intervertebral disc. It may present in children with back pain and refusal to walk. Growing pains (Choice C) are idiopathic and occur bilaterally at night in a nonarticular distribution. They are not accompanied by any abnormal examination findings. Hypermobility syndrome (Choice D) presents with joint hypermobility and associated joint and muscle pain. lliotibial band syndrome (Choice E) is caused by friction between the iliotibial band and lateral femoral epicondyle. It occurs most commonly as an overuse injury in athletes and presents with lateral knee pain. Ligamentous injury (Choice F) of the knee, such as injury to the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments, typically occurs as an acute sports injury and presents with abrupt knee pain and swelling. Osgood-Schlatter disease (Choice G) refers to osteochondrosis or traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that typically occurs in adolescent, athletic children. It presents with anterior knee pain and swelling. Osteoid osteoma (Choice H) are benign bony tumors that commonly occur in long bones and present with pain and refusal to bear weight. Patients would not present with fever or signs of sepsis. Osteomyelitis (Choice I) is an infection of bone and bone marrow. Patients typically complain of pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema. This patient's examination is more suggestive of an infection of the joint space, rather than of adjacent bone.

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy has progressive acute myelogenous leukemia despite numerous therapeutic interventions . During a meeting with his parents to discuss the prognosis and the futility of further treatment , his parents request that the patient not be told his prognosis . During an examination when his parents are not present, the patient asks if he is going to die soon. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: "Have you talked to your parents about this?
choices.B: "I have talked to your parents about this, and they do not want you to know.
choices.C: "Most children with your condition live a long time.
choices.D: "No one really knows. It's hard to say.
choices.E: "That's not the spirit I like to see in my patients.

correctExplanation: The disclosure of a fatal prognosis to pediatric patients is extremely challenging and requires careful balancing of the ethical imperatives to tell the truth, to involve the child in care, and to integrate the family's wishes along with the child's development and mental capabilities. Legally, minors are not considered to be autonomous decision makers and authority to determine what is in the child's best interest lies with the child's parents. In the case of nondisclosure requests by parents, any disclosure to the child should only be made with parental involvement and consent. In response to this child's question, it is best to gauge what discussion has taken place with the child's parents and to probe the child's level of understanding.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Choice B is likely to create conflict between the child and the parents. It also implies that there is significant information being concealed from the patient. Choices C and D are not truthful responses. While the clinician has an ethical obligation to respect the wishes of the parents, the clinician must also abide by the ethical imperative not to lie. A more careful deflection by asking probing questions is a better response to this child's question. Choice E is patronizing and fails to acknowledge the substance of this child's legitimate question. Failing to acknowledge the question inhibits the child's ability to participate in or understand their own care. Educational Objective: The authority for disclosure of medical information to children rests with the child's parents. In the event of a nondisclosure request, disclosures may only be made with parental consent.

questionStem: A newborn is examined 12 hours after birth for excessive oral secretions and coughing following his first feeding . The symptoms resolve after suctioning . Polyhydramnios was diagnosed by ultrasonography at 35 weeks' gestation. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated . He was delivered at term with no complications . Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . He weighs 3005 g (6 lb 10 oz). Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Newborns with esophageal atresia typically present with the inability to feed, with associated gagging and an inability to manage oral secretions. As well, since the fetus is unable to swallow amniotic fluid, the pregnancy may be complicated by polyhydramnios. Esophageal atresia often occurs with a concomitant tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The presence of a TEF, depending on the subtype, potentially conveys an increased risk for aspiration pneumonia and respiratory distress. Initial evaluation requires an attempt at insertion of a nasogastric tube and evaluation of its position with a chest x-ray. If the nasogastric tube remains coiled within the esophagus, this suggests the presence of esophageal atresia. Air within the gastrointestinal tract immediately after birth and prior to feeding suggests the existence of a TEF distal to the esophageal atresia. Definitive management requires surgical repair. Additional screening for associated congenital malformations should occur.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Genetic testing (Choice A) can be used to evaluate for chromosomal disorders, such as Down syndrome. While esophageal atresia is associated with malformation syndromes, it is not commonly correlated with a specific genetic abnormality. Ultrasonography of the abdomen (Choice B) can be used to evaluate for pyloric stenosis and intussusception, among other disorders. As the esophagus typically terminates in the thorax in the setting of esophageal atresia, ultrasonography of the abdomen does not play a role in its diagnosis. CT scan of the chest (Choice C) could potentially outline the patient's anatomy and characterize the esophageal atresia; however, placement of a nasogastric tube and chest x-ray would effectively provide the diagnosis while exposing the patient to less radiation. Laryngoscopy (Choice D) is the process of using a laryngoscope or camera to examine the larynx of the patient. As laryngoscopy does not evaluate the esophagus, it does not play a role in the evaluation of esophageal atresia. Educational Objective: Esophageal atresia presents with an inability to feed and manage oral secretions. If present along with a tracheoesophageal fistula, the patient may present with gagging, coughing, respiratory distress, and cyanosis in the neonatal period. Inability to pass a nasogastric tube with it remaining coiled in the proximal esophagus on chest x-ray is diagnostic. Definitive management requires surgical repair.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of a mass in the right side of the neck, progressive axillary and inguinal adenopathy , and generalized pruritus . She has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period . Examination shows no other abnormalities . An x-ray of the chest shows a mediastinal mass. Laboratory studies show anemia with a normal leukocyte count and differential , increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and increased serum ferritin concentration . A node biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: Hodgkin disease is a type of lymphoma, predominantly B-cell in origin, that occurs commonly in patients who are 20 to 30 and 55 to 65 years old. Patients typically present with lymphadenopathy, as well as nonspecific constitutional symptoms, such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, and pruritus. The most common sites of lymphadenopathy are the neck and mediastinum. Laboratory values typically demonstrate a normal leukocyte count, anemia, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and increased serum ferritin concentration, which are related to the underlying systemic inflammation. Initial evaluation commonly includes a chest x-ray or CT scan, which will potentially outline the extent of the patient's mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Definitive diagnosis requires excisional lymph node biopsy, which will disclose Reed-Sternberg cells (atypical cells with bilobed nuclei), a large inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophilic predominance, and fibrosis. Hodgkin cells are typically CD15- and CD30-positive. The most common subtype is nodular sclerosing, whereas the worst prognosis occurs in the setting of the lymphocyte-depleted subtype. Risk factors for its development include Ebstein-Barr infection, immunosuppression, and a family history of Hodgkin disease. Treatment includes chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cytomegalovirus infection (Choice A) is often asymptomatic but can cause a short febrile, flu-like illness in healthy patients. It can cause severe infections in immunocompromised patients. It does not present with generalized pruritus. Sarcoidosis (Choice C) is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition that can affect multiple organ systems, especially the lungs and lymphatic system. It typically presents with a cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and potentially with anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias. Thymoma (Choice D) is a benign or malignant tumor of the thymus. It presents with an anterior mediastinal mass, which can cause chest pain or shortness of breath. It is commonly associated with myasthenia gravis. It does not often present with lymphadenopathy. Tuberculosis (Choice E) is spread via airborne transmission and can present with a primary, latent, or reactivation pattern. Primary disease demonstrates subacute fever, weight loss, nights sweats, cough, and malaise, whereas latent tuberculosis is commonly asymptomatic. Reactivation presents similarly to primary disease but occurs after a period of latency, typically affecting the lung apices or resulting in miliary disease. Educational Objective: Hodgkin disease is a type of lymphoma, predominantly B-cell in origin, that demonstrates a bimodal age distribution. It typically presents with lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and pruritus. Evaluation commonly shows mediastinal lymphadenopathy, as well as Reed-Sternberg cells on histology.

questionStem: A 4½-year-old boy has periorbital and pedal edema and ascites 7 days after an upper respiratory tract infection . Breath sounds are diminished on the right side of the chest. His liver is palpable , and there is 2+ pretibial edema . Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine 44% 6 mg/dl 0.5 mg/dl Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no occult blood, WBCs , RBCs, casts, glucose , or ketones . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria. Minimal change disease appears normal on light microscopy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute glomerulonephritis (Choice A) can refer to a variety of glomerular diseases that involve inflammation of glomeruli, which typically present with hematuria, red blood cell urine casts, and hypertension. The patient has severe proteinuria and no RBCs in his urine, making this diagnosis unlikely. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Choice B) is a cause of nephrotic syndrome that can result in proteinuria and pitting edema. FSGS is commonly associated with sickle cell disease, opioid use, and HIV, and is characterized by segmental sclerosis of the glomeruli that is visible on light microscopy. lgA nephropathy (Choice C) is characterized by episodic hematuria that occurs concurrently with upper respiratory tract infections. When lgA deposition occurs in the renal mesangium, glomerulonephritis may ensue, causing microscopic hematuria, erythrocyte casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria. Membranous nephropathy (Choice D) is a nephrotic syndrome which is more common in adults and can be secondary to drugs (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), infections (eg, hepatitis B and C), or systemic lupus erythematosus. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Educational Objective: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and lower extremities, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria. Minimal change disease appears normal on light microscopy.

questionStem: A 9-month-old boy has pneumonia for the fourth time . He was born at 28 weeks' gestation with a grade 4 intraventricular hemorrhage and generalized neurologic devastation . Barium swallow shows a grade 4 gastroesophageal reflux. Which of the following operative procedures is most likely to decrease the frequency of recurrent pneumonia?
correctExplanation: The inhalation of orogastric contents is known as aspiration, and it can occur from simple fluids such as water, or from stomach contents as a result of emesis or gastroesophageal reflux, as in this patient. The aspiration of acidic stomach contents may cause aspiration pneumonitis, whereas the aspiration of gastrointestinal flora and bacteria can cause aspiration pneumonia. The volume of aspirate is a strong predictor of complications from aspiration, especially in the case of pneumonia, as the bacterial inoculum may overwhelm the native ability of pulmonary alveolar defense (macrophages, cilia, mucus) to prevent colonization, replication, and infection. Aspiration pneumonia classically presents with a cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, and rhonchi on physical examination. Imaging classically shows an infiltrate in the most dependent lung segments at the time of aspiration (eg, in the superior segment of the inferior lobe when supine or lower lobes when erect). Patients at a higher risk for aspiration include those with impaired airway-protective reflexes (eg, neurological injury, myasthenia gravis, altered mental status), frequent or forceful emesis, abnormal pharyngeal or airway anatomy or function (eg, malignancy, tracheoesophageal fistula), or severe gastroesophageal reflux. Options for the management of severe gastroesophageal reflux in children include dietary changes and proton pump inhibitors or histamine- 2 receptor antagonists, although these would not assist in decreasing the risk for aspiration pneumonia. Fundoplication is a surgical procedure that improves the gastroesophageal sphincter tone by wrapping the fundus around the distal esophagus, which decreases the frequency and severity of reflux.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Esophagostomy (Choice A) is a surgical opening into the esophagus that is occasionally used in head and neck cancer to provide enteral nutrition. It does not play a role in the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux. Gastrostomy (Choice C) is the surgical creation of an opening into the stomach, which can be used for enteral nutrition or to remove the contents of the stomach via drainage. For this to be effective in preventing aspiration caused by gastroesophageal reflux, the placed tube would have to be placed to suction or to drainage at all times, which would prohibit proper nutrition. Fundoplication is a more reasonable option. Pyloromyotomy (Choice D) is a procedure that decreases the strength of the pyloric sphincter. It is used to treat hypertrophic pyloric stenosis but is not used in the management of severe gastroesophageal reflux. Vagotomy and pyloroplasty (Choice E) entails the surgical ligation of the vagus nerve, in addition to the enlargement of the pyloric opening, which is used to treat gastric ulcers. These procedures would not prevent aspiration in this patient. Educational Objective: Aspiration pneumonia is typically secondary to impaired airway reflexes, abnormal oropharyngeal or tracheal anatomy or function, or severe gastroesophageal reflux with regurgitation of gastric contents. Recurrent aspiration from severe gastroesophageal reflux can be treated with fundoplication, which tightens the gastroesophageal sphincter and decreases the frequency and severity of reflux.

questionStem: Over the past 48 hours, an 8-week-old boy has been vomiting continuously after each meal. The emesis is projectile and does not contain bile. The infant appears lethargic and has dry mucous membranes . Palpation of the abdomen shows a small olive-sized mass in the epigastric region . Which of the following profiles is most likely in this infant?
correctExplanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is a disorder of the pyloric sphincter that occurs in young infants and can result in partial or complete gastric outlet obstruction. It is caused by hypertrophy of the pylorus and an inability to relax the pyloric sphincter. Infants classically present within the first 1 to 2 months of life with forceful nonbilious emesis. Physical examination is notable for a characteristic ovoid mass in the epigastric region. The recurrent emesis, if severe, may result in signs of volume depletion and malnutrition. Laboratory studies typically show a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium ions. Additionally, the resultant volume depletion causes activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in renal losses of potassium and protons. Confirmatory diagnosis is made by ultrasound imaging to evaluate the thickness and length of the pyloric muscle. Patients are treated with surgical pyloromyotomy to relieve the stenosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Choices A and B are incorrect as they represent metabolic alkalosis with a high chloride concentration. Metabolic alkalosis that results from the loss of gastric acid typically results in hypochloremia as a result of the loss of chloride ions. Choices D and E are incorrect as they represent hypochloremic acidosis and not an alkalosis as would be expected with the high-volume loss of gastric acid and contraction alkalosis. There are numerous causes of metabolic acidosis, and the differential can be narrowed by evaluating for a normal or high anion gap. Educational Objective: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a disorder marked by hypertrophy of the pylorus that can result in gastric outlet obstruction. A hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis results from the loss of gastric acid and potassium ions, along with contraction alkalosis caused by the severe volume depletion.

questionStem: A 3-year-old African American girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of worsening , diffuse abdominal pain and loss of appetite . During this time, she has had a 1-kg (2-lb) weight loss. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a firm, nodular midline mass from the mid to upper abdomen . There is pain and swelling of the right wrist. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . An x-ray of the abdomen and ultrasonography of the mass show a 12-cm midline mass with multiple calcifications . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neuroblastoma is a neoplasm of neuroendocrine cells of the sympathetic nervous system. It may arise from any sympathetic nervous tissue and is the most common tumor of the adrenal gland that occurs in children. Other locations include the sympathetic chain. Adrenal involvement classically presents with abdominal pain and distention, weight loss, and failure to thrive. Patients may also present with an associated paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome. Physical examination may show a firm, nodular mass that crosses the midline and diastolic hypertension. Diagnosis is suggested by the presence of increased catecholamine metabolites in the serum and urine. Neuroblastoma is associated with overamplification of the MYCN oncogene. Histologic characteristics include small round blue cells that may form rosette patterns clustered around a central lumen, with positive stains for bombesin and neuron-specific enolase markers. Neuroblastoma commonly metastasizes to bone and skin. Treatment and prognosis are dependent on the stage of the tumor at diagnosis and the presence or absence of MYCN amplification.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Ewing sarcoma (Choice A) is a primary bone malignancy driven by t(11 ;22) chromosomal translocation. On histology, Ewing sarcoma demonstrates multiple small, round, blue cells. X-rays may demonstrate elevated periosteum and layered neocortex formation. It often occurs in the long bones (eg, femur, tibia) and typically presents in adolescence. Multicystic dysplastic kidney (Choice B) is a nonhereditary pediatric cystic renal disease that results from the formation of multiple renal cysts in utero. It is typically sporadic. It can affect one or both kidneys, with a higher incidence of bilateral involvement in females. The affected kidney is replaced by numerous cysts and retains no functioning renal tissue. Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) (Choice D) is the most common renal malignancy in childhood. It occurs secondary to mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass and hematuria. It does not typically cross midline and is often smooth to palpation rather than nodular. Polycystic kidney disease (Choice E) refers to either autosomal recessive or dominant polycystic kidney disease. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease is a form of infantile cystic renal disease that manifests with the development of numerous small renal cysts that replace the normal renal parenchyma, resulting in end-stage kidney disease. It typically has a variable age of presentation during fetal life or childhood but can be a potential cause of oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence) if it develops in utero. Educational Objective: Neuroblastoma is a malignancy of neuroendocrine cells of the sympathetic nervous system that commonly affects the adrenal glands. It may be differentiated from other common abdominal malignancies of childhood by its tendency to cross the mid line and have a nodular texture, along with its association with paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and increased concentrations of serum and urine catecholamine metabolites.

questionStem: A 12-hour-old male newborn has not urinated since birth. He was born at 36 weeks' gestation to a 15-year-old primigravid patient and weighed 2325 g (5 lb 2 oz). Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . His mother received no prenatal care. During her pregnancy, she smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily and occasional marijuana and drank approximately two beers on the weekends . Since birth, the newborn has received one ounce of cow's milk-based formula without vomiting and has passed one small meconium stool. He is alert and active . His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 135/min, and respirations are 35/min . Examination shows no dysmorphic features . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Heart sounds are normal. The lower abdomen is distended with a midline mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Congenital urinary tract abnormalities include but are not limited to unilateral renal agenesis, fused kidneys, ureteral stricture and stenosis, duplex collecting system, posterior urethral valves, bladder agenesis, bladder exstrophy, hypo- or epispadias, and urethral strictures. Posterior urethral valves are formed from an abnormal remnant of the Wolffian duct and can result in urinary tract obstruction. This is often diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography showing bladder distention, hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios, and a fetus that is small for gestational age. In this patient who is premature, underweight, and has not voided, a midline mass is likely a distended bladder secondary to posterior urethral valves that were not diagnosed prenatally. Complications including rupture of a calyx around the kidney, or intraperitoneal bladder rupture. Definitive diagnosis of posterior urethral valves is made with voiding cystourethrography showing dilation, elongation, and tapering of the urethra. Treatment is with endoscopic valve ablation.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Alcohol toxicity (Choice A) in pregnancy can result in fetal alcohol syndrome, which can cause intellectual disability and congenital abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (eg, thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures), and heart defects. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (Choice B) defines a variable state of disease related to adrenal hypofunction that results in decreased concentrations of cortisol with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. The presentation varies depending on the age of onset, severity, and gender of the patient. In rare, mild cases, infertility may be the only presenting complaint when declared in adolescence or young adulthood. Most cases of CAH are diagnosed in childhood. Meconium ileus (Choice C) occurs when abnormally thick meconium occludes the intestine, resulting in a bowel obstruction. It is associated with cystic fibrosis. This patient has already passed meconium. Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) (Choice D) is the most common renal malignancy in childhood resulting from mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass and hematuria. Testicular torsion (Choice F) occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow. This can lead to testicular infarction if not promptly managed. Educational Objective: Posterior urethral valves are formed from an abnormal remnant of the Wolffian duct and can result in urinary tract obstruction. Signs and symptoms can include bladder distention, hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios, and a fetus that is small for gestational age.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of increasing difficulty breathing . His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 116/80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention and mild swelling of the face and upper extremities . There are moderate intercostal retractions . lnspiratory and expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows a mass in the superior mediastinum and a large pleural effusion in the right hemithorax . Thoracentesis yields 400 ml of reddish brown serosanguineous fluid containing numerous erythrocytes . Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pleural effusion?
correctExplanation: The patient is most likely presenting with a malignant pleural effusion. His physical examination findings of jugular venous distention and edema of the face and upper extremities are suggestive of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, which is caused by obstruction of the SVC and venous congestion of the upper body and face. Obstruction of the SVC is often caused by extrinsic compression by a malignant mediastinal or pulmonary mass, which may be secondary to lung cancer, lymphoma, or metastatic disease from another primary source. Pleural effusions are clinically suspected on examination in the setting of dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds, and can be visualized on imaging including chest x-ray, CT scan, or ultrasonography. Analyzing the pleural fluid can show an underlying cause to guide therapy. Fluid is inspected for cell counts, organisms, pH, enzyme activity, and serum glucose concentration and total protein concentrations. Low pH and low serum glucose are indicative of increased cellular metabolism in the fluid and may indicate underlying malignancy and/or infection. Malignant pleural effusions may have increased erythrocyte counts or appear grossly hemorrhagic as a result of tumor invasion and disruption of blood vessels and the visceral pleura. As well, Light criteria assesses whether the pleural effusion is likely to be exudative (eg, complex fluid resulting from pneumonia, empyema, malignancy, or inflammatory disease) or transudative (eg, serous fluid resulting from imbalanced hydrostatic or oncotic pressures) through evaluating the concentrations of pleural fluid protein and lactate dehydrogenase.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Congestive heart failure (Choice A) and nephrotic syndrome (Choice C) may be complicated by transudative pleural effusions caused by volume overload. Pleural effusions associated with volume overload are most likely bilateral as a result of the underlying systemic derangement, while exudative effusions related to malignancy or infection are more commonly unilateral. As well, transudative effusions do not demonstrate increased erythrocyte, lactate dehydrogenase, or protein concentrations. Traumatic hemothorax (Choice D) is an exudative effusion that contains increased erythrocyte concentrations and may appear frankly bloody on thoracentesis. It often occurs in the setting of rib fractures and/or pulmonary contusions. Malignant pleural effusion is more likely in the setting of a mediastinal mass on imaging. Tuberculous pleural effusion (Choice E) may be seen in endemic regions in the setting of chronic tuberculosis infection. The pleural fluid is characteristically exudative, with a high lymphocyte count and an increased adenosine deaminase concentration. Educational Objective: Pleural effusions may be categorized as transudative or exudative based on the Light criteria. Increased protein or cells in the fluid indicates an exudative transfusion. Malignancy is a common cause of exudative pleural effusions, with lymphoma the most likely cause in a child with an underlying mediastinal mass.

questionStem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of vomiting and drooling . She had been left alone in the bathroom of her home for a few minutes before the onset of the symptoms . The family keeps nasal decongestants , acetaminophen , ibuprofen , diphenhydramine , drain cleaner, and insecticide spray in the bathroom . During the past 5 days, she has had an upper respiratory tract infection treated with a nasal decongestant containing pseudoephedrine and acetaminophen . She is agitated and drooling . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 26/min , and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Examination shows two small superficial ulcers on the lips and tongue . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . The most likely cause of these findings is ingestion of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Drain cleaners are a common cause of caustic ingestions in children. They contain sodium and potassium hydroxides, alkali that are proton acceptors and strong nucleophiles. Alkali ingestion leads to liquefactive necrosis, lactic acidosis, and tissue penetration and ulceration. It can cause chemical burns and ulcerations of the tongue, airway, and esophagus, resulting in stridor, hoarseness, vomiting, and drooling.
