If severe, esophageal perforation can result leading to free air in the mediastinum. Treatment is initially focused on supportive measures including airway management and fluid resuscitation. Visible lesions in the oropharynx increase the likelihood of distal gastrointestinal lesions. Patients should be evaluated with endoscopy to assess for visceral injury. For severe injuries, treatment involves steroid administration.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acetaminophen (Choice A) toxicity is characterized by acute liver failure. At high doses, saturation of phase II metabolic pathways leads to excess acetaminophen being metabolized by cytochrome P450-mediated reactions to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which has strong oxidizing properties and is directly hepatotoxic. Diphenhydramine (Choice B) ingestion results in central nervous system H1-receptor blockade, anticholinergic, and anti-a-adrenergic side effects. This results in a constellation of symptoms such as dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, hallucinations, delirium, ataxia, flushed skin, visual disturbances (cycloplegia), and sedation. Ibuprofen (Choice D) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits cyclooxygenase. In small doses, it can cause impaired gastric mucosal protection resulting in gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. In large overdose or ingestion, ibuprofen can cause hypotension, hypothermia, and metabolic acidosis; however, this is uncommon. Organophosphates (Choice E) are found in insecticides; exposure can occur transcutaneously, or via inhalation or ingestion. They are a cause of cholinergic excess as they inhibit acetylcholinesterase, which is characterized by vomiting, diarrhea, urination, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, seizures, and muscle weakness. Pseudoephedrine (Choice F) is a sympathomimetic that activates the adrenergic receptor system and is used as an over-the-counter nasal decongestant because of its effects on nasal vasoconstriction. Ingestion and toxicity can cause nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, restlessness, and anxiety. Educational Objective: Drain cleaners contain caustic alkali that can cause burns and ulcerations of the tongue, airway, and esophagus, resulting in stridor, hoarseness, vomiting, and drooling.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of left hip pain for 2 days and an associated limp for the past 4 hours. One week ago, he had watery stools and temperatures to 37.8°C (100°F); these symptoms resolved within 2 days. There is no history of trauma or recent immunizations . He is otherwise healthy, and his immunizations are up-to-date . He appears alert. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. The left hip is not swollen or erythematous , but there is pain with movement and weight bearing . His erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 28 mm/h. Ultrasonography of the left hip joint shows a small effusion . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: The most likely diagnosis in this otherwise healthy patient is transient synovitis of the hip. Transient synovitis is an inflammatory condition involving the synovial lining of weight-bearing joints, with the hip being commonly affected. It classically presents in children recovering from a viral infection with pain on weight-bearing, antalgic gait, refusal to ambulate, tenderness over the joint, and pain elicited with range of motion. Vital signs are generally within normal limits, as are laboratory studies with the exception of increased markers of inflammation such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Antecedent viral infection has been reported in up to 30% of cases of transient synovitis. Diagnosis involves the exclusion of emergent or urgent conditions such as cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and fracture. Treatment is supportive, and involves rest plus nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, making oral ibuprofen the best choice for this patient. If there is diagnostic uncertainty, arthrocentesis to exclude septic arthritis, along with imaging to assess for osteomyelitis or fracture should be conducted.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oral acyclovir (Choice A) is appropriate for cases of herpetic infections, such as herpes labial is, genital herpes, or varicella infections. Acyclovir is a guanosine analog that must first be activated by viral thymidine kinase, and ultimately prevents replication of the viral genome. It demonstrates no independent anti-inflammatory properties. Oral clindamycin (Choice B), an antibiotic that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, is appropriate for treating cases of skin and soft-tissue infections, and exhibits broad activity against many gram-positive, gram­ negative, and anaerobic pathogens. Intravenous ceftriaxone (Choice D) and intravenous vancomycin (Choice E) are appropriate for the inpatient treatment of bacterial infections and are a common empiric regimen used to treat meningitis. Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, has a broad spectrum of activity against gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a common cause of migratory polyarthritis. Vancomycin inhibits the synthesis of bacterial cell walls, and therefore has the greatest activity against gram-positive organisms. It would be an appropriate choice to treat osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, or skin and soft-tissue infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Educational Objective: Transient synovitis is a noninfectious arthropathy that presents with pain of weight-bearing joints, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. Diagnosis involves the exclusion of emergent or urgent conditions such as cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and fracture. It is best managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician for an evaluation of short stature and delayed puberty. She has never had a menstrual period . Since birth, the patient's height has been below the 3rd percentile , and her weight has been at the 3rd percentile . At the age of 10 years , x-rays of the left hand and wrist showed that bone age was equal to chronologic age. Her mother, who is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall, had menarche at the age of 12 years . Her father is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall. The patient is 147 cm (4 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m 2• Her pulse is 76/min , and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg. Examination shows multiple nevi over the face and trunk . There is bilateral pedal edema . Breast development is Tanner stage 1, and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 1. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Gonadal dysgenesis 45, X (Turner syndrome) results from monosomy of the X chromosome and presents with characteristic physical features including short stature, a wide webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and multiple melanocytic nevi. Short stature in patients with Turner syndrome likely results from haploinsufficiency of the short stature homeobox gene on the X chromosome. Delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics is common, such as with the Tanner Stage 1 breast and pubic hair development in this patient. Primary amenorrhea is also a common finding. Patients with Turner syndrome may also present with bicuspid aortic valve, aortic coarctation, or a fused kidney.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease) (Choice A) may occur in pediatric patients and more commonly presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism. Thyroid dysfunction is less likely to result in delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics. Constitutional short stature (Choice B) may lead to short stature during childhood and adolescence but usually results in normal adult stature. This diagnosis would not account for the patient's finding of primary amenorrhea and delayed sexual development. Craniopharyngioma (Choice C) may lead to acquired deficiency of growth hormone. However, other accompanying findings are usually encountered, such as headache, vomiting, and visual field defects. Familial short stature (Choice D) is a common cause of short stature, but the child's expected height should be relatively similar to that of her parents. This child is both significantly shorter than both parents and has other findings, such as primary amenorrhea and delayed sexual development that would not be explained by this diagnosis. Idiopathic hypopituitarism (Choice F) may result in deficiency of one or several pituitary hormones, but it is a diagnosis requiring laboratory investigation and would not present with the remaining characteristic physical examination findings of Turner syndrome. Educational Objective: Gonadal dysgenesis 45, X (Turner syndrome) results from monosomy of the X chromosome and presents with characteristic physical features including short stature, a wide webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, multiple melanocytic nevi, primary amenorrhea, and delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics. Short stature in patients with Turner syndrome likely results from haploinsufficiency of the short stature homeobox gene on the X chromosome.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a well-child examination . His mother states that his belly seems big. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows aniridia . There is a palpable mass in the right flank . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Measurement of urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid concentrations

correctExplanation: Nephroblastoma, or Wilms tumor, is the most common renal malignancy in childhood as a result of mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. Patients can be asymptomatic or have symptoms of abdominal pain or hematuria. Nephroblastoma can also be associated with congenital anomalies such as hemihypertrophy, genitourinary abnormalities, and aniridia. The preferred initial diagnostic study is typically abdominal ultrasonography to evaluate the abdominal mass. Other masses that can be differentiated from nephroblastoma include hydronephrosis and polycystic kidney disease. If nephroblastoma is diagnosed, further imaging can be done to further evaluate any tumor infiltration and the full extent of the mass.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Measurement of serum catecholamine concentration (Choice A) can be performed in the evaluation of pheochromocytoma or neuroblastoma. Measurement of urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid concentrations (Choice B) is also performed in the evaluation of pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, tachypnea, and treatment-refractory hypertension. It is a common tumor of the adrenal medulla and is marked by the functional secretion of epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which cause episodic hyperadrenergic symptoms. X-ray of the abdomen (Choice C) can be performed to evaluate for bowel obstruction, swallowed foreign body, necrotizing enterocolitis, or constipation. An x-ray is not as sensitive as a CT scan and has little utility in the evaluation of abdominal masses. Chest imaging can elucidate whether there are any lung metastases. An x-ray of the chest (Choice D) would be less sensitive for this purpose, and the abdominal mass should be first evaluated. Educational Objective: Nephroblastoma is the most common pediatric renal malignancy and is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. The preferred initial diagnostic study is typically abdominal ultrasonography to evaluate the mass.

questionStem: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of lethargy, mild abdominal pain, and dark urine. He had a sore throat and an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago that resolved spontaneously . His pulse is 90/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows slight swelling around the eyes. Urinalysis shows light brown urine with RBC and granular casts. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings?

choices.B: Bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane
choices.C: Bacterial infiltration of the epithelial cells

correctExplanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by peripheral and periorbital edema, dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria following an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and subsequent complement activation and inflammation. Neutrophilic infiltration of the glomerular tuft can be seen in PSGN. Management of PSGN is supportive and focused on treating complications such as volume overload and hypertension with diuretics and antihypertensive medications. Rarely, severe kidney injury secondary to PSGN may require kidney replacement therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The pathogenesis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis involves antigen-antibody immune complex deposition, not direct bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane or epithelial cells (Choices B and C). Destruction of tubular epithelial cells (Choice D) describes the pathophysiology of acute tubular necrosis. Acute tubular necrosis typically occurs following an ischemic (Choice E) or nephrotoxic insult to the kidneys, which results in necrosis of the tubular epithelium. Granular, muddy brown casts are typical on urinalysis. Educational Objective: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a nephritic syndrome characterized by peripheral and periorbital edema, dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria following an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and subsequent complement activation and inflammation.

questionStem: A 2370-g (5-lb 3-oz) newborn is delivered at term to a 37-year-old primigravid woman who had limited prenatal care. The mother drank one to two beers daily but did not use any illicit drugs . The newborn appears vigorous and is not cyanotic . Examination shows a prominent occiput , narrow palpebral fissures , a small recessed mandible , and a short sternum . The hands are clenched with the index finger folded over the middle finger and the small finger folded over the ring finger. There is a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur that is heard best at the lower left sternal border. The abdomen is prominent and soft; there is no hepatosplenomegaly . Peripheral pulses are normal. There is generalized hypertonia . Deep tendon reflexes are present. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this newborn's low birth weight?
correctExplanation: Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, presents with characteristic physical features including intellectual disability, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched overlapping fingers, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles. It is the second most common trisomy in infants and is associated with decreased serum PAPP-A and 13-human chorionic gonadotropin concentrations in the first trimester. Treatment involves correction or management of life-threatening abnormalities. Most patients die within the first 6 months of age. In most cases, it is caused by a meiotic nondisjunction, which occurs when two chromatids fail to separate and a single haploid gamete contains two copies of a chromosome instead of one. The incidence of meiotic nondisjunction increases with increasing maternal age.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arthrogryposis (Choice A) describes congenital joint contractures, which result in impaired joint movement and function and may lead to muscle atrophy. Congenital infection (Choice B) can occur with multiple viruses such as cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), rubella, measles, or parvovirus. Each congenital viral infection results in different congenital abnormalities. HSV can cause both cutaneous herpetic lesions and systemic manifestations like meningoencephalitis. Congenital infection with CMV manifests as hearing loss, seizures, a petechial rash, intracranial calcifications, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Neonates with congenital rubella infection exhibit a classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease. Exposure to alcohol in utero (Choice C) results in fetal alcohol syndrome, which can cause intellectual disability and congenital abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (eg, thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures), and heart defects. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) describes insufficient blood flow to the placenta, abnormal placenta, or inability of the placenta to deliver sufficient nutrients to the fetus during pregnancy. It can result in a variety of disorders including fetal hypoglycemia, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, or maternal complications including preeclampsia, miscarriage, or stillbirth. Educational Objective: Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, presents with characteristic physical features including intellectual disability, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched overlapping fingers, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of intermittent severe abdominal cramping over the past 3 days . He has had no vomiting but has passed three stools during this period; the third stool had reddish discoloration . He is currently alert and resting comfortably . His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds . There is no organomegaly or masses . Test of the stool for occult blood is positive . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: lntussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools. Classically, it presents in an infant or young child with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain often punctuated by asymptomatic periods. lntussusception typically occurs as a result of the presence of a pathologic lead point, often lymphoid hyperplasia, lymphadenopathy, Meckel diverticulum, stricture, or malignancy, which acts to draw one segment of bowel into an adjacent segment during peristalsis. If the intussusception self-resolves, there may be no symptoms. If it does not resolve, traction on mesenteric vessels can result in hypoperfusion of the segment with resultant inflammation, hemorrhage, obstruction, and pain. It may be detected on physical examination as an elongated mass, often in the right upper quadrant. Diagnosis consists of clinical history and physical examination and is supported by imaging. Ultrasonography evaluation is preferred in young children and will show telescoping interposed bowel segments in longitudinal orientation or a targetoid appearance in transverse orientation. Treatment of an ileocolic intussusception requires the administration of a contrast enema, which decreases the intussusception. Contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this setting. Surgery may be required in cases where there is repetitive failure of the enema to decrease the intussusception or if the patient presents with symptoms concerning for bowel necrosis or perforation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Gastritis (Choice A) can be caused by a viral illness or use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is characterized by epigastric discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or if severe, hematemesis. The associated pain is typically constant. Juvenile polyps (Choice C) are benign hamartomas that can present with painless rectal bleeding. Abdominal pain would be uncommon. In a patient with severe abdominal cramping followed by bloody stool, intussusception is more likely. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) (Choice D) is uncommon in children and can be related to NSAIDs or He/icobacter pylori infection. Patients typically present with epigastric discomfort, nausea, and vomiting, typically after eating. PUD can be complicated by hemorrhage or perforation. Viral gastroenteritis (Choice E) is a common, typically self-limiting illness in children characterized by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and mild abdominal discomfort. It would usually not cause bloody stools. Bloody diarrhea in children should raise suspicion for bacterial gastroenteritis by Escherichia coli O157:H?. Educational Objective: lntussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he is concerned that he has not had to begin shaving . He says all of his friends have begun shaving . He first noticed pubic hair development 6 months ago. He is at the 25th percentile for height and 20th percentile for weight. Examination shows mild bilateral gynecomastia . Genital and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Puberty in boys typically follows a predictable course of gonadarche (enlargement of the testes), followed by pubarche (pubic hair), followed by adrenarche (axillary hair, facial hair, voice changes), followed by a growth spurt. This differs from the process in girls, which proceeds from thelarche (breast buds) to pubarche to growth spurt and finally menarche. In boys, delayed puberty is defined as the absence of testicular enlargement or secondary sexual characteristics at the age of 14 years. The most common cause of delayed puberty is constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), accounting for approximately 50% of cases, a normal variant. In CDGP, there is a transient defect in the production of gonadotropin-releasing hormone with resultant delay in the stimulation of pituitary production of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. CDGP tends to be familial with many members of the same family undergoing late puberty compared with peers. In this case, the patient has undergone gonadarche (indicated by his Tanner stage 2 genital development) and pubarche but has not yet undergone adrenarche. Thus, while delayed, the sequence of his procession through the steps of puberty is appropriate and he can be reassured that his development will continue to progress.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum testosterone concentration (Choice B) is unnecessary in this case because the patient is progressing through the stages of puberty as expected. If his puberty did not continue to progress, testosterone measurement could be used to differentiate CDGP from another pathology. Mild bilateral gynecomastia can be normal in early puberty as a result of the small increase in extragonadal production of estrogen relative to the amount of testosterone being produced. Urine toxicology screening (Choice C) would be appropriate if there was a suspicion for drug use inducing gynecomastia, of which marijuana is the most common recreational drug. Breast biopsy (Choice E) would be indicated if the breast enlargement was caused by a nodule or mass rather than true gynecomastia. If delayed puberty were accompanied by neurologic findings or suspected to be caused by a process involving the brain such as a pituitary adenoma, MRI of the brain, not CT scan of the head (Choice D), would be indicated. Neither imaging modality is necessary in this case. Educational Objective: In boys, puberty follows a predictable course of gonadarche, pubarche, and growth spurt. Delayed puberty is defined as the absence of testicular enlargement or secondary sexual characteristics at the age of 14 years and is most commonly caused by constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

questionStem: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of mild itching of his head and scattered areas of hair loss on his scalp. Examination shows several small oval areas of alopecia over the posterior scalp with numerous hairs broken off close to the scalp. Several small, occipital , nontender lymph nodes are palpated . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that is common in children. It presents as scaly patches with alopecia, patches of alopecia with black dots that represent broken hairs, and cervical lymphadenopathy. The most common causal organism is Trichophyton tonsurans, although infections can also be caused by other Trichophyton species, Microsporum species, and Epidermophyton species. A potassium hydroxide preparation of a skin scraping will show fungal hyphae or spores. It is treated with oral antifungals, such as griseofulvin or terbinafine.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Candida albicans (Choice A) can cause a variety of infections, such as oral thrush, esophagitis, and vulvovaginal candidiasis. It can also cause systemic infections in immunocompromised patients. It does not cause tinea capitis. Epidermophyton floccosum (Choice B) is a dermatophyte that can cause skin and nail infections, such as tinea pedis and tinea corporis. It less commonly causes tinea capitis. Ma/assezia furfur (Choice C) causes tinea versicolor, a superficial fungal infection of the skin that commonly presents with areas of hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, or macules on the trunk and proximal upper extremities. It does not cause tinea capitis. Microsporum audouinii (Choice D) is a dermatophyte that causes skin infections, such as tinea capitis and tinea corporis. However, it is a less common causal pathogen than Trichophyton tonsurans in tinea capitis. Educational Objective: Tinea capitis presents commonly in children with scaly patches, hair loss, and cervical lymphadenopathy. A frequent causal organism is Trichophyton tonsurans.

questionStem: A 12-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of chickenpox for 4 weeks . She developed vesicular lesions on her head, trunk, and extremities 2 weeks after her older brother developed lesions , and she has continued to have new lesions since then. She is at the 10th percentile for length, weight , and head circumference . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4 °F). Examination shows pa pules, fluid-filled vesicles , and crusted small ulcers scattered over the head, trunk, and proximal extremities . Indirect fluorescent antibody testing of the material from the base of one of the vesicles is positive for the varicella antigen . Which of the following is the most likely immunologic abnormality?
correctExplanation: Varicella zoster, also known as human herpesvirus-3, is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions. It causes the disease chickenpox in immunocompetent children and can cause encephalitis and pneumonia in immunosuppressed children. The rash associated with chickenpox typically persists for 1 to 2 weeks. Varicella is uncommon in infancy and may occur as an opportunistic infection in infants with HIV or as an immunocompromising condition impairing T lymphocytes. As with many viral infections, T lymphocyte function is an essential component of host defense and is impaired in the setting of HIV infection. Persistence of symptoms for 1 month is suggestive of underlying T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. Infants with immunodeficiency are at a greater risk for severe consequences of varicella infection, including end organ involvement.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Impaired B-lymphocyte function (Choice A) occurs in several immunodeficiencies such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia and common variable immunodeficiency. Affected infants demonstrate recurrent infections with both bacterial and viral organisms. Impaired complement function (Choice B) occurs in several complement disorders. Patients with deficient function of complement are at increased risk for infection with encapsulated bacterial organisms. Impaired neutrophil adhesion (Choice C) occurs in leukocyte adhesion deficiency. Patients present with recurrent skin and mucosal infections, absent pus, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord. Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis (Choice D) occurs in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which presents with albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and recurrent pyogenic infections. Neutrophil oxidation burst (Choice F) defects occur in chronic granulomatous disease, which presents with recurrent infections with organisms possessing catalase, such as Staphylococcus aureus. Educational Objective: Defense against varicella zoster virus relies on T lymphocyte function, which is impaired in the setting of HIV infection and T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. Infants with deficient T lymphocyte function are at an increased risk for severe infection with varicella, which may manifest as persistent infection or end organ involvement.

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has developed several brown spots on the skin since birth . Her 28-year-old mother has similar spots as well as several 1-cm subcutaneous lumps and scoliosis . Examination of the girl shows four 1-cm flat brown spots on the back . Which of the following is the most likely pattern of inheritance in this patient?
correctExplanation: Neurofibromatosis 1 is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder that typically results from an inherited mutation of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. Neurofibromatosis 1 is inherited with complete penetrance and variable expressivity. Rarely, the mutation in the NF1 gene occurs sporadically. The disorder presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), cafe au lait spots, axillary or inguinal freckling, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and/or pheochromocytomas. The diagnosis is typically based on physical examination findings, but genetic testing may be utilized to confirm ambiguous cases. Treatment includes surgical debulking of tumors, management of seizures and neurological complications, and genetic counseling.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Autosomal recessive neurocutaneous disorders (Choice B) include ataxia-telangiectasia, which presents with oculocutaneous telangiectasias, progressive cerebellar ataxia, immune deficiency, and neurologic abnormalities. Mitochondrially inherited disorders (Choice C) rarely include neurocutaneous findings. Mitochondrial diseases typically present with muscle weakness, encephalopathy, and incoordination. The inheritance pattern of neurofibromatosis 1 is not multifactorial (Choice D) or unknown (Choice F). It is known to be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with complete penetrance and variable expressivity. X-linked recessive neurocutaneous disorders (Choice E) include Menkes disease, a congenital X-linked disorder that causes a defect in intestinal copper absorption, leading to copper deficiency. The disease presents with progressive neurologic symptoms, hypopigmentation of the skin, bony abnormalities, and kinked hair. Educational Objective: Neurofibromatosis 1 is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder that typically results from an inherited mutation of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene. The disorder presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), cafe-au-lait spots, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and/or pheochromocytomas.

questionStem: A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever and agitation for 8 hours. She has had an upper respiratory tract infection for 2 days . Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min , and blood pressure is 60/palpable mm Hg. An S3 gallop is heard on auscultation . S 1 and S2 are normal. Scattered crackles are heard bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's findings?
correctExplanation: Viral myocarditis can present in children with fever and signs and symptoms characteristic of heart failure, including volume overload, chest pain, shortness of breath, pulmonary edema noted as crackles auscultated in the lungs, and an S3 gallop on physical examination. In addition, patients may also present with arrhythmias, exercise intolerance, syncope, hypotension, tachypnea, and tachycardia. An S3 gallop is a heart sound associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure as a result of increased atrial and ventricular end-diastolic volume. Children may have a viral prodrome of fever, malaise, and myalgia or a recent respiratory or gastrointestinal illness prior to the onset of myocarditis. Treatment of children with myocarditis focuses on supportive care to maintain perfusion and hemodynamic stability, including diuretics and noninvasive or mechanical ventilation if necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bronchiolitis (Choice A) is a respiratory tract infection commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Although it can cause respiratory distress as a result of mucous plugging of small airways, it does not cause volume overload, pulmonary edema, or an S 3 gallop. Rhonchi, not crackles, are typically heard on lung auscultation. Endocarditis (Choice B) is a rare disease in children that is usually associated with an underlying congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, or central venous catheter use. It involves vegetations that form on the endocardium or valves and can present with fever, new murmur, vegetation seen on echocardiography, or blood cultures growing microorganisms typical of endocarditis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Choice C) can be asymptomatic, may present with syncope on exertion, or may present with signs of heart failure as in this patient, but typically in a subacute or chronic course. Patients may also have exertional chest pain or arrhythmias. On examination, a systolic murmur can be heard as a result of the left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Fever and an S3 gallop are more suggestive of myocarditis. Mitral valve rupture (Choice E) can lead to pulmonary edema, shortness of breath, and tachypnea. However, it is not commonly associated with fever unless it presents as a complication of endocarditis, and is characterized by a systolic murmur on auscultation, not an S3 gallop. Educational Objective: Viral myocarditis can present in children with fever and signs and symptoms characteristic of heart failure, including volume overload, chest pain, shortness of breath, pulmonary edema noted as crackles auscultated in the lungs, and an S3 gallop on physical examination.

questionStem: A 9-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of lethargy, labored breathing, and seven episodes of vomiting over the past 6 hours. Her skin is flushed and warm and she appears severely dehydrated . There is a fruity odor to her breath. She is at the 75th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds , and capillary blood glucose concentration is greater than 500 mg/dl . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose in wate
choices.B: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 0.9% saline
choices.C: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer solution with 40 mEq/L of potassium chloride
choices.D: Intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin
choices.E: Continuous intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin

correctExplanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as ~-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs as a result of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Extracellular hyperglycemia creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying profuse osmotic diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Patients present with signs and symptoms including tachycardia, tachypnea, fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, Kussmaul respiration, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Laboratory evaluation typically shows increased concentrations of glucose, ketones, and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions (ketones, lactic acid) in serum. Treatment is through the replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Insulin is typically repleted at an initial dose of 0.1 U/kg/hour by intravenous infusion. Volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline is essential to restore intracellular fluid volume and lower the extracellular glucose concentration and is the initial step in the management of DKA even prior to insulin administration. Administering insulin prior to knowing the serum potassium concentration can result in life-threatening hypokalemia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose in water (Choice A) would worsen this patient's profound hyperglycemia. 0.9% saline is a more appropriate initial resuscitation fluid. Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer solution with 40 mEq/L of potassium chloride (Choice C) may be acceptable once the patient's potassium concentration is known; however, in DKA, derangements in potassium can include hypo- or hyperkalemia. Infusing a fluid with potassium may result in worsening of unknown derangements with potentially life-threatening dysrhythmias. Administration of regular insulin either via intravenous dose at 0.1 U/h (Choice D) or via continuous intravenous infusion at 0.1 U/h (Choice E) is not the best next step because neither of these options are adjusted for the patient's weight. Insulin is typically repleted at an initial dose of 0.1 U/kg/h by intravenous infusion. Intravenous volume repletion with 0.9% saline is therefore a more appropriate initial step. Additionally, insulin repletion is only appropriate in DKA once the serum potassium concentration is known to prevent precipitating life-threatening derangements in potassium. Educational Objective: Extracellular hyperglycemia in the setting of diabetic ketoacidosis creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Restoration of fluid balance is an essential step in the emergent management of diabetic ketoacidosis and is best accomplished with the intravenous administration of 0.9% saline.

questionStem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a diffuse rash for 24 hours . She has had cough , congestion , eye discharge , and fever for 4 days . The rash initially began on her face and chest but has spread to involve her abdomen , back , and lower extremities . Her temperature is 38.9°C(102 .1 °F), pulse is 100/min , respirations are 16/min , and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a diffuse red, macular and papular rash involving the face , trunk , and extremities ; there are no lesions on the palms or soles . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: F) Rocky Mountain spotted fever G) Rubeola H) Scabies I) Scarlet fever J) Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome Measles (rubeola) virus is a highly contagious paramyxovirus that causes the disease measles, which is associated with acute febrile illness and potentially severe sequelae. It is more common in children than adults. It characteristically presents with a prodromal fever along with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a confluent maculopapular rash that starts at the head/neck and spreads to the trunk, excluding the palms and soles. Physical examination may show bright red macules with a bluish-white center on the buccal mucosa (Koplik spots) and lymphadenopathy. Treatment is supportive. Vitamin A deficiency is associated with severe disease and complications, and supplementation should be provided, especially in children who are malnourished. Complications of measles include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (a neurodegenerative disease associated with intellectual regression, personality changes, motor deterioration, seizures, and premature death), encephalitis, and giant cell pneumonia.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Ehrlichiosis (Choice A) is a tick-borne illness with a wide spectrum of disease characteristics, including fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, and altered mental status. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Choice B) is an acute, systemic, small-vessel vasculitis that occurs in children and typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (eg, buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain. It often occurs following a viral illness or upper respiratory tract infection. Id reaction (Choice C) is a manifestation of type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. It often presents as a diffuse eczematous rash triggered by inflammation of the skin at a single site, such as soles in the presence of tinea pedis or the hands in dyshidrotic eczema. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) (Choice D) is a multisystemic vasculitic disease resulting in acute arteritis with a risk for the development of coronary artery aneurysms. In children, the disease is characterized by fever for at least five days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Pityriasis rosea (Choice E) is a cutaneous eruption characterized by the acute onset of a pruritic patch followed by the development of numerous smaller macules and patches. It commonly involves the trunk and proximal extremities. It may be induced by a viral infection. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Choice F) is a tick-borne Rickettsial disease caused by the organism Rickettsia rickettsii, which presents with a petechial rash that starts at the ankles and wrists. It is classically accompanied by headache and fever, but not cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis. Scabies (Choice H) is a skin infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei that is transmissible by skin-to-skin contact, as in family members or sexual partners. The skin infestation typically occurs on the sides or webs of the fingers, wrists, axillae, areolae, or genitalia and leads to intense pruritus. Scarlet fever (Choice I) can present with an erythematous tongue, rash, and desquamation of hands and feet. The rash of scarlet fever is characteristically a rough, papular, diffuse body rash. Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome (Choice J) is characterized by a full-body, erythematous, desquamating rash with accentuation in the skin folds. It is caused by production of exfoliative toxin by Staphylococcus aureus.

questionStem: A 5-year-old girl with a 1-year history of chronic nonproductive cough is brought for a follow-up examination . The cough occurs during the day and night and is not exacerbated by exercise . She has not had chills, diarrhea , or weight loss. Inhaled 13-adrenergic agonists , two courses of oral antibiotics , and a 10-day course of oral prednisone have not relieved her symptoms . She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. She appears well. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 96/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 82/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities except for a linear consolidation in the right middle lobe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Bronchiectasis refers to dilation and distortion of the bronchi or bronchioles that leads to obstructive lung disease. There are numerous causes in children, including congenital bronchiectasis resulting from underlying genetic disorders of cartilage or the airways, cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, recurrent aspiration, airway malignancies, immunodeficiency syndromes with recurrent necrotizing pulmonary infections, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and connective tissue disorders. Children classically present with chronic cough (with or without sputum production) and symptoms of infection (fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) during exacerbations. Exercise intolerance and dyspnea on exertion are usually absent until late in disease progression. Associated symptoms and physical examination findings are dependent on the underlying cause. Chest imaging may show linear atelectasis or scarring, dilated airways with thickened walls, and peripheral opacities related to multifocal mucous plugs. Bronchiectasis may result in a progressive decline in pulmonary function, if untreated, and manifest as a severe, chronic obstructive lung disease that limits a patient's activity. Lung transplantation may be required later in life.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. arAntitrypsin deficiency (Choice A) results in the early development of panacinar emphysema and cirrhosis. It is a hereditary disease resulting from misfolding of arantitrypsin. The lack of functional arantitrypsin release results in an imbalance of proteases and antiproteases in the lung parenchyma, resulting in the destruction of alveolar septa and development of panacinar emphysema. Asthma (Choice B) is characterized by reversible obstruction to airflow caused by the spasm of smooth muscle in the bronchi and small airways, and may present with dyspnea, wheezing, or chronic nonproductive cough. It is often triggered by an allergen (eg, smoke, pollen), exercise, or temperature change. It may be associated with progressive reactive airway remodeling over time. The lack of response to inhaled 13- adrenergic agonists and oral prednisone in this patient do not support the diagnosis of asthma. Congenital emphysema (Choice D) is a rare pulmonary disorder caused by disrupted embryonic bronchopulmonary development and is characterized by air trapping and lung hyperinflation, which can be visualized on chest imaging. The severity of disease varies widely and may be asymptomatic until adulthood or present in the newborn with respiratory distress. Cystic fibrosis (Choice E) is a clinical syndrome resulting from defects in the CFTR gene, leading to a deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. Cystic fibrosis is associated with bronchiectasis because of the risk for recurrent pulmonary infections. The absence of other findings associated with cystic fibrosis, such as pancreatic insufficiency, diarrhea, malnutrition, and weight loss, argue against cystic fibrosis as the cause of this patient's bronchiectasis. Educational Objective: Bronchiectasis is an obstructive lung disease characterized by dilation and thickening of the bronchi or bronchioles. It has numerous associated causes, including cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and immunodeficiencies with recurrent necrotizing pulmonary infections. Chronic cough is a typical presenting symptom in children.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician requesting contraceptive advice . She feels well. She is currently sexually active with two male partners and uses condoms inconsistently . Menarche was at the age of 12 years , and menses occur at regular 35-day intervals and last 5 days . Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m 2• Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min , and blood pressure is 105/65 mm Hg. Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows an ectropion on the cervix . The external genitalia , vaginal mucosa , uterus, and adnexa are normal. In addition to initiating a conversation about contraceptive methods and performing a Pap smear, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
choices.C: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone concentrations
choices.D: Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine concentrations

correctExplanation: In this healthy, adolescent female, preventative measures will primarily address her sexual health. The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening all sexually active adolescent women under the age of 25 years for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Chlamydia trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted disease that can cause various infections including cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, and urethritis. However, in most cases it is asymptomatic and thus screening asymptomatic individuals is important for disclosing and treating active infections before long-term sequelae develop. Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae also commonly co-infect the same individual. This patient's examination demonstrates cervical ectropion, which develops when there is slight eversion of the cervix to expose a portion of the endocervix and its columnar mucosa to the vaginal canal. In young women, it is a normal variant and does not warrant treatment, although it does increase the risk for acquiring sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing (Choice A) is not indicated until a patient reaches the age of 30 years old. Prior to that time, cytologic study of cells collected from the cervix alone is adequate for the screening of cervical cancer. After the age of 30, cervical cancer screening may be performed by cytologic study every 3 years or by cytologic study combined with HPV testing every 5 years. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone concentrations (Choice C) is unnecessary since this patient does not demonstrate signs of delayed puberty. There are no indications to suggest an abnormality in this patient's hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine concentrations (Choice D) is unnecessary and not indicated for screening in an asymptomatic individual. Measurement of these laboratory values would be indicated if the patient were showing signs or symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Colposcopy (Choice E) is a procedure in which the cervix is visualized under magnification for the purpose of identifying cancerous or precancerous areas to obtain diagnostic samples. Colposcopy is indicated as a follow-up to an abnormal cervical cancer screening test or to further evaluate abnormal findings on initial cervical examination. This patient's ectropion is common in adolescents and is considered a normal variant. There is no indication for colposcopy in this patient. Educational Objective: The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening all sexually active adolescent women under the age of 25 years for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections. Early identification of these often asymptomatic infections will prevent long-term sequelae from developing. Cervical ectropion is a normal variant and does not warrant treatment, although it does increase the risk for acquiring sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV.

questionStem: A 12-year-old boy falls out of a tree and sustains a fracture of the shaft of his right humerus . He is unable to extend his wrist or fingers . The most likely diagnosis is injury to which of the following?

choices.B: Posterior cord of the brachia! plexus

correctExplanation: The radial nerve is a nerve of the brachia! plexus with contributions from the C5-T1 nerve roots. It courses through the axilla, down the posterior shaft of the humerus within the spiral groove, and then along the posterolateral aspect of the forearm. It provides sensation to the posterior upper extremity and the dorsal hand, as well as motor sensation to the extensors of the elbow, wrist, and fingers. It is prone to injury with midshaft humerus fractures, as it runs in close proximity to the humeral diaphysis within the spiral groove.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The musculocutaneous nerve (Choice A) courses along the anterolateral portion of the arm and is responsible for sensation over the lateral forearm, as well as elbow flexion and forearm supination. This patient is unable to extend his wrist and fingers, which is more typical of a radial nerve injury. The posterior cord of the brachia! plexus (Choice B) contributes to the subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subcapsular, axillary, and radial nerves. While an injury to the posterior cord of the brachia! plexus would present with loss of wrist and finger extension, it would also be expected to cause weakness of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the shoulder, in addition to other symptoms. The median nerve (Choice C) courses along the anteromedial arm and through the carpal tunnel to the hand. It is responsible for sensation to the volar aspect of the lateral 3 ½ fingers, as well as wrist flexion, lateral finger flexion, and thumb opposition. It is most commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus given its course, not in midshaft humerus fractures. The ulnar nerve (Choice E) courses along the medial aspect of the arm. It provides sensation to the volar aspect of the medial 1 ½ fingers, as well as wrist flexion, medial finger flexion, finger abduction, and finger adduction. It is most commonly injured in medial epicondyle fractures of the humerus, not midshaft fractures of the humerus. Educational Objective: The radial nerve is commonly injured in midshaft fractures of the humerus as it courses in the spiral groove. Radial nerve injuries typically present with the inability to extend the elbow, wrist, or fingers, along with the loss of sensation to the posterior arm and dorsal hand.

questionStem: A 4-day-old newborn is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of progressive jaundice . He was born at 36 weeks' gestation to a 27-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 2, following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 2608 g {5 lb 12 oz). The newborn's blood group is 0 , Rh-positive , and the mother's blood group is B, Rh-positive . He has been breast-fed since birth and receives 1 to 2 ounces of a supplemental soy milk-based formula every day. His mother says that he has had about seven wet diapers daily, and his stools are yellow and seedy. At discharge 2 days ago, his weight was 2495 g (5 lb 8 oz); he now weighs 2608 g (5 lb 12 oz). His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 65/40 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus and jaundice from the face to the lower abdomen . The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory studies at 36 hours of age and now show: Hematocrit (%) Serum Bilirubin, total (mg/dl) Direct (mg/dl) At 36 Hours of Age Now 54 52 8.2 0.1 12.5 0.3 Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Neonatal jaundice is defined as an increased bilirubin concentration (greater than 5 mg/dl), which results from either increased hemolysis {bilirubin generation) or decreased bilirubin conjugation or excretion. Hyperbilirubinemia can be divided into direct and indirect forms in which either conjugated or unconjugated bilirubin accumulate, respectively. It can also be divided into physiologic and pathologic forms. Features of physiologic jaundice include development after 24 hours of life, a rate of bilirubin rise of less than 0.5 mg/dl daily, a maximum peak of 14 to 15 mg/dl, and a predominance of indirect bilirubin (greater than 90%). In contrast, jaundice within the first 24 hours of life {which rises faster than 0.5 mg/dl per hour), a predominance of direct bilirubin, and persistence beyond 2 weeks would suggest a pathologic cause. Newborn physiologic jaundice, also termed benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, occurs in nearly all newborns and is caused by the increased breakdown of red blood cells and thus generation of bilirubin, the immature liver metabolism of bilirubin, and the increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. These features taken together cause an indirect hyperbilirubinemia to develop. Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is closely monitored in order to prevent kernicterus, which refers to the deposition of bilirubin in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. This can occur at bilirubin concentrations of 25 to 30 mg/dl. Treatment of the underlying cause of the jaundice and phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia or exchange transfusion prevents this potentially fatal consequence.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. ABO isoimmunization {Choice A) occurs when maternal lgG antibodies to fetal red blood cell antigens cause either fetal or neonatal destruction of these red blood cells. Bilirubin production is increased, and an indirect hyperbilirubinemia ensues. This cause of neonatal jaundice will present with pathologic findings such as an early presentation and rapid rate of rise, neither of which are present in this case. Biliary obstruction {Choice B) caused by biliary atresia is a common cause of direct hyperbilirubinemia. In congenital biliary atresia, the common bile duct is occluded or atretic and bile is unable to pass into the duodenum. Dehydration {Choice C) is the mechanism behind breastfeeding jaundice. In the first week of life, as a breastfeeding mother's milk begins to establish, the infant may become dehydrated. Dehydration leads to increased enterohepatic circulation and reabsorption of bilirubin, resulting in indirect hyperbilirubinemia. In this case, the infant's consistent wet diapers and stools argue against a dehydrated state. Erythrocyte enzyme defect {Choice D) such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes increased hemolysis of red blood cells and a subsequent increase in unconjugated bilirubin.
