questionStem: A 4-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of a 6-hour history of fever, decreased alertness , and a rash over her chest, arms , and legs. On admission , the patient is obtunded . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 70/30 mm Hg. Examination shows a purple macular rash over the trunk and extremities . The face and extremities are edematous . Fluid is administered by intravenous bolus, and intravenous administration of ceftriaxone and vancomycin is started . Fifteen minutes after admission , the patient becomes apneic . She is intubated , and mechanical ventilation is started . Serum studies show: Her urine output is 1.5 mUkg/h . Arterial blood gas analysis on 40% oxygen shows : Na• K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Creatinine 135 mEq/L 4 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 35 mg/dl 0.8 mg/dl 7.2 35 mm Hg 100 mm Hg One hour later, her urine output decreases to less than 0.5 mUkg/h . A chest x-ray shows hazy lung fields bilaterally and cardiomegaly . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous administration of an isotonic fluid bolus

correctExplanation: A patient with fever, hypotension, edematous extremities, cardiomegaly, decreased urine output, and respiratory distress raises suspicion for myocarditis and cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock can occur when decreased cardiac output leads to organ hypoperfusion. In cardiogenic shock, dysfunction of cardiac myocytes results in decreased chronotropy, lusitropy, or inotropy. Decreased cardiac output and increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure result from such dysfunction. Systemic vascular resistance is increased as a physiologic attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure in the setting of decreased cardiac output and peripheral perfusion. Physical examination findings can include tachycardia, tachypnea, crackles on auscultation of the lungs, and an S3 or S4 gallop on cardiac auscultation. Dopamine is a vasopressor and inotrope at increased doses. Intravenous administration of dopamine may be appropriate in cases of cardiogenic shock or refractory hypotension.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of an isotonic fluid bolus (Choice A) is typically done initially in cases of distributive or hypovolemic shock. It would be harmful in a patient with cardiogenic shock because of impaired cardiac output and exacerbation of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and it was already empirically attempted in this case. Intravenous administration of furosemide (Choice C) would not be an initial step in the management of cardiogenic shock. Although total body fluid volume is increased (eg, pulmonary edema and extremity edema), cardiac output to the kidneys is decreased. Restoration of cardiac output and mean arterial pressure to prevent further damage to organs is the first priority. Intravenous administration of nitroprusside (Choice D) would be detrimental to this patient who is hypotensive. Nitroprusside is an intravenous, titratable vasodilator that can be used for the treatment of hypertensive emergencies. It breaks down in circulation to release nitric oxide, which in turn activates guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle to result in vascular smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation. Increased inhaled oxygen concentration (Choice E) would not be beneficial to this patient. Arterial blood gas analysis of this patient shows adequate partial pressure of oxygen.

questionStem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of swelling of his lower lip that has slowly resolved during the past 2 days. He has a 12-month history of intermittent asymmetric swelling of his face , chest, and arms . During three of the episodes , he also had abdominal pain and diarrhea . There is no history of travel outside the USA. He takes no medications . He does not use illicit drugs . He is not sexually active. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Measurement of serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity
choices.C: Measurement of serum C1 esterase inhibitor concentration

correctExplanation: Hereditary angioedema presents with intermittent episodes of swelling of the skin, face, and lips, as well as the mucosal lining of the respiratory and gastrointestinal system. It is caused by an autosomal dominant­ inherited or de novo deficiency in C1 esterase inhibitor, which leads to overactivation of the complement system and overproduction of bradykinin. Bradykinin is a vasodilator that leads to the symptoms associated with hereditary angioedema. Episodes of angioedema can be caused by trauma, medications, and infections. They are not improved by antihistamines but commonly self-resolve. Further evaluation would also demonstrate a decreased C4 complement concentration in addition to the decreased concentration or activity of serum C1 esterase inhibitor.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Skin testing for environmental allergies (Choice A) may be useful in the evaluation of allergic reactions or anaphylaxis, which may also present with angioedema. However, anaphylaxis also causes wheezing as a result of laryngeal edema, urticaria, emesis, and hypotension. It is generally acute in onset following a specific exposure. Measurement of serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity (Choice B) would not be useful in the evaluation of hereditary angioedema. However, decreased activity of ACE, as can be caused by ACE inhibitor medications, can lead to angioedema as a result of the decreased degradation of bradykinin. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in hereditary angioedema. Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) (Choice D) is a test used to identify antibodies against particular antigens, although it is no longer commonly used. Because hereditary angioedema is not caused by an allergic reaction, a RAST would not be useful in its evaluation beyond ruling out an allergic contributor which is unlikely on the basis of no specific exposure history. Serum protein electrophoresis (Choice E) is commonly used to evaluate for malignancy (eg, multiple myeloma), as well as kidney and immunological disorders. It is not frequently used to evaluate the complement system and, thus, would have no role in diagnosing hereditary angioedema. Educational Objective: Hereditary angioedema presents with recurrent episodes of swelling of the skin, face, lips, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract. It is caused by a deficiency in C1 esterase inhibitor, which leads to the overproduction of bradykinin, a vasodilator.

questionStem: A previously healthy 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department in January because of cough and poor feeding for 2 days. She is still urinating and making tears. She initially had a fever of 38.2°C (100.8°F) but has been afebrile for the past day. She appears mildly ill. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 56/min . Examination shows pink tympanic membranes with good mobility. There are mild intercostal retractions , and diffuse bilateral crackles and wheezes are heard . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Culture of the pharynx for bacteria

correctExplanation: Bronchiolitis is a common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in children under the age of 2 years. It is typically caused by a viral infection, commonly from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It presents with a viral prodrome of fever, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea followed by cough, dyspnea, and lethargy as inflammation progresses to the lower airway. Auscultation may disclose wheezes and crackles. Severe disease is marked by the presence of increased respiratory effort (tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, grunting), hypoxemia, and apnea. Patients presenting with severe disease should be hospitalized and immediately started on respiratory support with the administration of oxygen, nasal suctioning, and advanced airway and ventilatory support if respiratory failure is imminent.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Arterial blood gas analysis (Choice A) may confirm the presence of hypoxemia but should not delay the administration of oxygen given the patient's decreased peripheral oxygen saturation. Culture of the pharynx for bacteria (Choice B) is indicated for the workup of pharyngitis, which may present with fever, sore throat, and dysphonia. Causes include group A streptococcus, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and viruses. Viral culture of respiratory secretions (Choice C) may be included in the diagnostic workup to identify influenza, RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, or other causal agents. This information can aid decision-making for the use of pharmacologic therapies, isolation precautions, and prophylactic treatment of exposed contacts. Oxygen should be administered first. X-rays of the chest (Choice D) and neck (Choice E) may be obtained to exclude alternative diagnoses for respiratory distress such as epiglottitis, bacterial pneumonia, pneumothorax, foreign body aspiration, or heart failure. The initial step in management is securing the airway and treating the patient's hypoxemia. Administration of an inhaled bronchodilator (Choice F) may be considered in the emergency setting if there is ambiguity of the underlying diagnosis and concern for reactive airways disease. It does not particularly help with the treatment of bronchiolitis. As well, supplemental oxygen should be administered first in a patient with hypoxemia. Subcutaneous administration of epinephrine (Choice H) is not a currently accepted therapy for bronchiolitis. Oxygen should be administered first. Subcutaneous epinephrine may be appropriate in the treatment of anaphylaxis or reactive airway disease. Educational Objective: The initial management of hypoxemia requires the administration of supplemental oxygen, regardless of cause. Bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in children less than 2 years of age, often secondary to infection with RSV. Treatment entails supplemental oxygen, frequent nasal suctioning, and consideration of an advanced airway if severe.

questionStem: A previously healthy 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother's boyfriend 30 minutes after she stopped breathing . He says that prior to giving her a bath, she suddenly cried, became limp, and stopped breathing . She is unresponsive , flaccid , and cyanotic . Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.?°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 5/min , and palpable systolic blood pressure is 45 mm Hg. The pupils are fixed and dilated . Funduscopic examination shows bilateral retinal hemorrhages . After securing an airway, a CT scan of the head shows bilateral cerebral edema and acute interhemispheric subdural hemorrhage . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Severe intracranial injury with a history inconsistent with the severity of the patient's physical findings raises suspicion for abusive head trauma and nonaccidental trauma. Patients with abusive head trauma can present with encephalopathy, apnea, seizures, and retinal hemorrhages, and can have associated injuries such as rib fractures, long bone fractures, or skull fractures. Risk factors for nonaccidental trauma include unstable family situations, prior history of abuse, major birth defects, and parental depression. The mechanism of abusive head trauma is typically inflicted by blunt force trauma or shaking, which results in an acceleration-deceleration force on the infant. Infants are more vulnerable to deceleration injury because of several factors. The large head and weak neck musculature result in greater movement of the brain in the intracranial space when acted upon by acceleration and deceleration force such as in shaking. In addition, the infant skull is thin and flat, allowing forces to transfer through the skull to the brain. CT scan findings that are associated with nonaccidental head trauma include subdural hemorrhage (especially multiple hemorrhages or those in an interhemispheric or posterior fossa location), hypoxic-ischemic injury, and cerebral edema.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Apparent life-threatening event (Choice B) is a transient and unexpected change in an infant's breathing, appearance, or behavior. It is typically resolved by the time infants present for medical evaluation, and the history involves a brief episode of cyanosis or pallor, abnormal or absent breathing, marked change in tone, or altered level of consciousness. Aspiration (Choice C) can present in infants as choking or coughing during feeding. Infants may also have apnea during feeding or failure to thrive resulting from insufficient intake and feeding difficulty. It would be unlikely to cause acute encephalopathy and intracranial injury. Blunt trauma head injury (Choice D) can be severe enough to cause altered level of consciousness, behavioral changes, and vomiting. Infants with unintentional head trauma would present with a history consistent with head injury. Retinal hemorrhages, subdural hemorrhage, and cerebral edema are more significantly associated with abusive head trauma than with unintentional head injury. Near drowning (Choice E) in infants can result in aspiration, hypoxemia, respiratory distress, and laryngospasm. Hypoxemia leads to ischemic neuronal damage resulting in cerebral edema. However, retinal hemorrhages and subdural hemorrhage are more likely to be secondary to abusive head trauma. Suffocation (Choice F) can result in hypoxia, hypercarbia, loss of consciousness, and severe neurologic injury including seizures and coma. Other physical signs may include petechiae on the eyelids and bruising around the neck. Educational Objective: Patients with abusive head trauma can present with encephalopathy, apnea, seizures, and retinal hemorrhages, and can have associated injuries such as rib fractures, long bone fractures, or skull fractures. The mechanism of abusive head trauma is typically inflicted by blunt force trauma or shaking, which results in an acceleration-deceleration force on the infant.

questionStem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He is feeding well. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Immunizations are up-to-date . His vital signs are within normal limits. The lungs are clear to auscultation . A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border with radiation throughout the precordium . A systolic thrill is palpated at the lower left sternal border. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities . Femoral pulses are equal. An ECG shows no abnormalities . An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged left atrium . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ventricular septal defects (VSD) are among the most common congenital heart malformations, and they may occur in isolation or in association with complex structural abnormalities. The genetic cause of VSDs is heterogeneous and includes known associations with well-defined syndromes such as Down, DiGeorge, or Holt-Oram syndrome. It may also occur in isolation and via nonspecific, random mutations and individual point mutations that are de nova. VSDs are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border and may have an associated palpable thrill. VSDs result in a left-to-right shunt, which increases pulmonary blood flow. This leads to remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature and resultant smooth muscle hypertrophy. In turn, concentric narrowing of the pulmonary arterioles occurs, which results in the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension. If severe and progressive enough, this can cause increased right ventricular pressures and associated myocardial hypertrophy, which subsequently results in reversal of the shunt, presenting with shortness of breath and cyanosis. Increased pulmonary blood flow also results in increased blood return to the left atrium, which may cause left atrial enlargement.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Aortic stenosis (Choice A) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, best heard at the upper right sternal border and radiates to the carotid arteries. It classically occurs secondary to age-related fibrotic and calcific changes of the valve but can occur earlier in life in cases of bicuspid aortic valve or rheumatic heart disease. Atrial septal defect (Choice B) is a common congenital malformation of the interatrial septum resulting in a left-to-right shunt. Examination typically shows a fixed, widely split S2 caused by increased blood flow through the pulmonic valve. Severe defects can result in pulmonary hypertension and development of Eisenmenger syndrome over time, with reversal of the left-to-right shunt. Pulmonary valve stenosis (Choice C) presents with a systolic murmur best heard in the second left intercostal region, which is generally crescendo-decrescendo in nature, though quieter and with less radiation to the lower neck than aortic stenosis because of lower pressure in the pulmonary circulation. Tetralogy of Fallo! (Choice D) consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right-to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. The murmur heard with tetralogy of Fallo! relates to the underlying VSD characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border. This otherwise healthy patient without other findings more likely has an isolated VSD. Educational Objective: VSDs are common cardiac malformations that result in a left-to-right intracardiac shunt. They may form in isolation or in conjunction with other malformations. The majority are asymptomatic and will self-resolve, but severe disease can result in pulmonary hypertension and development of Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated.

questionStem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of coughing spells that have progressively worsened over the past 10 days and are frequently followed by vomiting . On examination , he is afebrile and appears healthy until he spontaneously has a coughing spell. Coughing continues for 20 seconds , at which time he appears cyanotic for 10 seconds . No crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Often, such coughing fits are accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis toxin is a major virulence factor that inactivates the G; subunits of G protein-coupled receptors in the respiratory epithelium and systemically, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP concentrations. In neutrophils and macrophages, this results in impaired recruitment, migration, and production of inflammatory mediators. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines (DTaP). It is treated with antibiotics, typically macrolides, and supportive care.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspiration caused by gastroesophageal reflux (Choice A) more commonly presents with symptoms in association with feeding and may also present with recurrent bacterial pneumonia and fever. Chlamydia! pneumonia (Choice B) may be preceded by neonatal conjunctivitis. It classically presents in infants with a staccato cough, in which each cough is separated by a brief inspiration. Physical examination may show tachypnea and crackles. Congestive heart failure (Choice C) in an infant is likely to be preceded by signs and symptoms of cardiac malformations or dysfunction during the neonatal period. While congenital heart defects may lead to cyanosis, severe paroxysms of coughing are atypical and are more suggestive of pertussis. Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis (Choice E) is more likely to present with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Patients may also display apneic episodes, although severe paroxysms of coughing would be atypical. Educational Objective: Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing, which may be accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization, and is treated with antibiotics, typically macrolides.

questionStem: A 7-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after the onset of vomiting bilious material. He has passed one bloody stool during this period . He has refused to feed for 12 hours. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . He was initially well except for occasional wet burps after breast-feeding . He appears lethargic . He weighs 3260 g (7 lb 3 oz). His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 65/35 mm Hg. Examination shows mottled skin and a supple neck. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and diffuse tenderness with guarding . Bowel sounds are decreased . On digital rectal examination , there is gross blood. A lateral x-ray of the upper gastrointestinal tract with barium contrast is shown . Which of the following events in utero is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.A: Abnormal exocrine secretions from the pancreas and intestinal glands
choices.B: Failure of cannulization of the proximal bowel
choices.C: Failure of caudal migration of ganglion cells
choices.E: Vascular occlusion in a segment of bowel

correctExplanation: Midgut volvulus, a dangerous complication of intestinal malrotation, often occurs in children within the first few months of life. Malrotation results from the incomplete rotation of the midgut during embryonal development and leaves the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. The cecum also remains in an abnormal position within the mid-upper abdomen instead of the right lower quadrant and is attached to the lateral abdominal wall by fibrous bands which cross over the top of the duodenum and can also cause constriction. This leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus at the base of the SMA. Volvulus can lead to bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and vascular compromise of the small bowel with consequent intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis. The SMA is susceptible to constriction in midgut volvulus because of its anatomical proximity and embryonal relationship to the formation of the midgut. Evaluation of malrotation and midgut volvulus requires an upper gastrointestinal barium study, which will outline the patient's small bowel anatomy and further assess for the presence of an obstructive volvulus. The upper gastrointestinal barium study in this patient demonstrates a spiral appearance of the duodenum with an abnormal position of the duodenojejunal junction on the lateral view, which indicates the presence of malrotation with a midgut volvulus. Treatment requires emergent surgical correction.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abnormal exocrine secretions from the pancreas and intestinal glands (Choice A) can occur in cystic fibrosis, which is caused by a failure of proper chloride channel function. This leads to inspissated stool and meconium ileus, which can present with abdominal distention but more commonly presents with absence of a bowel movement within the first 48 hours of life. It would not be expected to cause peritonitis, as in this patient. Failure of cannulization of the proximal bowel (Choice B) results in duodenal atresia. It typically presents with signs of intestinal obstruction in the newborn, such as recurrent emesis and poor feeding. It is associated with Down syndrome, polyhydramnios in utero, and a two adjacent contrast­ filled structures on imaging. This patient was previously able to tolerate oral feeding, making this diagnosis less likely. Failure of caudal migration of ganglion cells (Choice C) causes Hirschsprung disease, which classically presents with the failure to pass stool in the first 48 hours of life. Digital rectal examination commonly demonstrates an explosive release of stool, rather than gross blood, as in this patient. Vascular occlusion in a segment of bowel (Choice E) can result in jejunal or ileal atresia. This most commonly occurs in the setting of maternal smoking or use of cocaine. The newborn typically presents with poor feeding and emesis, and on imaging exhibits multiple air-fluid levels in the small bowel proximal to the site of atresia causing obstruction.
